verse.text: The revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave him to show his slaves what must soon take place. He made it known by sending his angel to his slave John,
verse.note: The Greek word is the ordinary term for a slave, a person owned by a master, and a first-century reader would have heard it that way. Most English versions use “servants,” partly because the Septuagint uses the word for the prophets as God’s devoted agents and partly because “slave” carries the weight of modern history. The term here expresses belonging and obedience, not degradation.
The Greek phrase can mean “soon” or “quickly,” that is, swiftly once it begins. Most translators choose “soon,” supported by “the time is near” in verse 3. The other reading is possible.

verse.text: who testified to the word of God and to the testimony of Jesus Christ, to everything he saw.
Blessed is the one who reads aloud the words of the prophecy, and blessed are those who hear and keep what is written in it, for the time is near.
verse.note: The contrast between one reader and many hearers shows that public reading is meant. Few people owned or could read books, so a document like this was read aloud to the gathered community by one person.

verse.text: John, to the seven assemblies in Asia: Grace to you and peace from the one who is and who was and who is coming, and from the seven spirits who are before his throne,
verse.note: The Greek word meant a gathering of people: a city’s citizen assembly, or in the Greek Old Testament, Israel assembled before God. “Church” is the near-universal rendering and is not wrong, but it now suggests a building or an institution. This translation uses “assembly” throughout so the reader sees the same word each time.
This is the Roman province of Asia, the western part of modern Turkey, not the continent. All seven cities named in verse 11 lay within it.

note.term: the one who is and who was and who is coming
note.traditional: him which is, and which was, and which is to come

verse.note: The Greek deliberately breaks normal grammar here, leaving the title in an unchanged form after “from,” as if it were a name that cannot be altered. “The one who is” echoes the Greek version of God’s self-naming to Moses in Exodus 3:14. The third element is literally “the coming one,” not “the one who will be.”

Many interpreters take this as a symbolic way of naming the Holy Spirit in fullness, since the phrase stands between God and Jesus Christ in a blessing. Others take the seven spirits to be seven chief angels before God’s throne, a figure known from Jewish writings. The translation keeps the literal wording and leaves the question open.

verse.text: and from Jesus Christ, the faithful witness, the firstborn of the dead, and the ruler of the kings of the earth. To him who loves us and freed us from our sins by his blood,
verse.note: The earliest and best manuscripts read “freed” (or “loosed”) us from our sins. Many later manuscripts read “washed,” a Greek word differing by one letter and pronounced almost identically, and this is what the King James Version follows. Nearly all modern editions and translations read “freed.”

verse.text: and made us a kingdom, priests to his God and Father—to him be the glory and the dominion forever and ever. Amen.
Look, he is coming with the clouds, and every eye will see him, even those who pierced him, and all the tribes of the earth will mourn over him. Yes, amen.

note.term: he is coming with the clouds

verse.note: The verse weaves together two Old Testament passages: Daniel 7:13, where one like a son of man comes with the clouds of heaven, and Zechariah 12:10, where people look on the one they pierced and mourn. “All the tribes of the earth” could also be read as “all the tribes of the land,” as in Zechariah, but Revelation’s scope here appears to be universal.

verse.text: “I am the Alpha and the Omega,” says the Lord God, “the one who is and who was and who is coming, the Almighty.”
I, John, your brother and partner in the affliction and kingdom and endurance that are in Jesus, was on the island called Patmos because of the word of God and the testimony of Jesus.
verse.note: The Greek is an ordinary word for hardship or oppression that bears down on people. “Tribulation” is the traditional rendering in Revelation, but many readers now hear it as the name of a specific end-time period, which says more than the word itself does. John speaks of it as something he and his readers already share.

verse.text: I was in the Spirit on the Lord’s day, and I heard behind me a loud voice like a trumpet,
verse.note: This is the earliest occurrence of the phrase. Most scholars take it to mean the first day of the week, Sunday, on which Christians met; that usage is clear in Christian writings soon afterward. A minority take it as the prophetic “day of the Lord,” but the Greek wording differs from the usual expression for that.

verse.text: saying, “Write what you see in a scroll and send it to the seven assemblies: to Ephesus and to Smyrna and to Pergamum and to Thyatira and to Sardis and to Philadelphia and to Laodicea.”
verse.note: The word means a written document, which in this period was normally a roll of papyrus. “Book” is the traditional rendering, but it suggests a bound volume with pages, which a first-century reader would not have pictured.

verse.text: I turned to see the voice that was speaking with me, and when I turned I saw seven golden lampstands,
and among the lampstands one like a son of man, clothed in a robe reaching to his feet and with a golden sash wrapped around his chest.

note.term: one like a son of man
note.traditional: one like unto the Son of man

verse.note: The Greek has no article and echoes Daniel 7:13, where “one like a son of man” means a figure of human appearance. Some translations capitalize the phrase as the title Jesus uses for himself in the Gospels. The figure is clearly the risen Jesus, but the wording here describes what John saw and is left as a description.

verse.text: His head and his hair were white like white wool, like snow, and his eyes were like a flame of fire,
his feet were like fine bronze, as if fired in a furnace, and his voice was like the sound of many waters.
verse.note: This Greek word is found only in Revelation (here and 2:18), and its exact meaning is unknown. It evidently names a gleaming metal or alloy of the copper family; “burnished bronze” and “fine bronze” are the usual guesses. The grammar of the following phrase is also irregular, but the picture of metal glowing in a furnace is clear.

verse.text: In his right hand he held seven stars, and from his mouth came a sharp two-edged sword, and his face was like the sun shining in its strength.
When I saw him, I fell at his feet as though dead. And he placed his right hand on me, saying, “Do not be afraid. I am the first and the last,

text.q: and the living one—I was dead, and look, I am alive forever and ever—and I have the keys of death and of Hades.
So write what you have seen, and what is, and what is going to take place after this.

As for the secret meaning of the seven stars that you saw in my right hand, and of the seven golden lampstands: the seven stars are the angels of the seven assemblies, and the seven lampstands are the seven assemblies.”

verse.note: The Greek word means a secret, here the hidden significance of a symbol that is then explained. Most English versions keep “mystery,” treating it as an established term. That word now suggests a puzzle or something beyond understanding, whereas here the meaning is stated plainly at once.

The Greek word means “messenger” and is used of both heavenly and human messengers. Elsewhere in Revelation it always refers to heavenly beings, so most scholars understand heavenly representatives or guardians of each assembly. Others take it as human messengers or leaders of the assemblies; the question remains disputed.

text.q: “To the angel of the assembly in Ephesus write: Thus says the one who holds the seven stars in his right hand, who walks among the seven golden lampstands:

verse.note: The Greek word was the ordinary term for a civic gathering and the Septuagint’s term for Israel assembled before God. “Church” now suggests a building or an institution, so this translation uses “assembly” throughout. Most translations keep “church,” which readers readily understand; “assembly” can sound like a single meeting, but here it means the community of believers in a city.

The word means both “angel” and “messenger.” Most interpreters take the “angel” of each assembly as a heavenly being who represents the community, in line with the angels elsewhere in the book; others take it as a human messenger or leader. The messages address the angel in the singular but plainly speak to the whole community. The speaker throughout the chapter is the risen Jesus of the vision in chapter one.

note.traditional: These things says; The words of

verse.note: The formula was already old-fashioned in first-century Greek. Readers knew it from the Septuagint, where it introduces the prophets’ “Thus says the Lord,” and it is also found in the proclamations of kings. Each of the seven messages opens with it, which gives them the tone of a prophetic oracle or a royal edict.

text.q: I know your works, your toil and your endurance, and that you cannot bear evil people. You have tested those who call themselves apostles and are not, and you have found them false.
You have endurance and have borne up for the sake of my name, and you have not grown weary.
But I have this against you: you have abandoned the love you had at first.
Remember, then, from where you have fallen; turn back and do the works you did at first. If not, I am coming to you and will remove your lampstand from its place—unless you turn back.

verse.note: “Repent” now centers on feeling sorry. The Greek word carries the prophets’ call to return to God, a change of direction in mind and conduct, which suits the command here to go back to the works done at first. Most translations keep “repent” as an established term that readers understand to include a change of life.

text.q: But this you do have: you hate the works of the Nicolaitans, which I also hate.
Let anyone who has an ear hear what the Spirit is saying to the assemblies. To the one who conquers I will grant to eat from the tree of life, which is in the paradise of God.

verse.note: The verb is the ordinary word for winning a battle, a contest or a court case, and is related to the noun for “victory.” “Overcome,” used by many translations, now tends to suggest merely getting past a difficulty. The meaning is not in dispute, and several modern versions also use “conquer” in Revelation.

text.q: “And to the angel of the assembly in Smyrna write: Thus says the first and the last, who was dead and came to life:
I know your affliction and your poverty—yet you are rich—and the slander from those who call themselves Jews and are not, but are a synagogue of Satan.

verse.note: The Greek is an ordinary word for hardship or oppression that bears down on someone, not a technical term. “Tribulation” is now heard by many readers as the name of a specific end-time period, which says more than the word does. The same word appears in verse 10 and in “great affliction” in verse 22.

John, himself Jewish, is describing a local conflict in Smyrna (and again in Philadelphia, 3:9), probably with members of the Jewish community who had spoken against the believers to their harm. The charge treats “Jews” as a name of honor that these opponents have forfeited, not as a term of reproach. Exactly who the group was is debated. The later use of the phrase against Jewish people in general is foreign to its setting.

text.q: Do not fear what you are about to suffer. Look, the devil is about to throw some of you into prison so that you may be tested, and you will have affliction for ten days. Be faithful to the point of death, and I will give you the crown of life.
Let anyone who has an ear hear what the Spirit is saying to the assemblies. The one who conquers will certainly not be harmed by the second death.
“And to the angel of the assembly in Pergamum write: Thus says the one who has the sharp two-edged sword:

I know where you live—where Satan’s throne is. Yet you hold fast to my name, and you did not deny your faith in me even in the days of Antipas, my witness, my faithful one, who was killed among you, where Satan lives.

verse.note: Pergamum was a leading center of emperor worship in the Roman province of Asia and home to famous sanctuaries, including a great altar of Zeus and a shrine of the healing god Asclepius. Which of these the phrase points to is uncertain; many interpreters think of the imperial cult, since refusing to take part in it could be dangerous. Nothing is known of Antipas beyond this verse.

text.q: But I have a few things against you: you have some there who hold fast to the teaching of Balaam, who taught Balak to put a stumbling block before the children of Israel, to eat food sacrificed to idols and to commit sexual immorality.

verse.note: The verb covers unlawful sexual relations generally, but in the Greek version of the prophets it is also a standard image for unfaithfulness to God through idolatry. The story alluded to (Numbers 25 and 31:16) joins the two: Israelite men slept with Moabite women and joined in their sacrifices. Whether the teachers at Pergamum and Thyatira promoted actual sexual license, or the word is a figure for taking part in idol feasts, is disputed; the translation keeps the literal sense.

text.q: In the same way, you too have some who hold fast to the teaching of the Nicolaitans.
Turn back, then. If not, I am coming to you soon and will make war on them with the sword of my mouth.

Let anyone who has an ear hear what the Spirit is saying to the assemblies. To the one who conquers I will give some of the hidden manna, and I will also give a white stone, and written on the stone a new name that no one knows except the one who receives it.

verse.note: The word means a pebble of the kind used for voting and counting. Suggestions for the image include the white pebble a juror cast to acquit, a token giving admission to a feast, and an amulet inscribed with a secret name. None can be shown to be the one intended, and the meaning remains uncertain.

text.q: “And to the angel of the assembly in Thyatira write: Thus says the Son of God, whose eyes are like a flame of fire and whose feet are like burnished bronze:

verse.note: The Greek word is known only from Revelation (here and at 1:15), and its exact meaning is unknown. It clearly names some gleaming metal or alloy of copper; “burnished bronze” is the usual approximation.

text.q: I know your works, your love and faith and service and endurance, and that your latest works are greater than the first.

But I have this against you: you tolerate that woman Jezebel, who calls herself a prophetess and who teaches and misleads my slaves into committing sexual immorality and eating food sacrificed to idols.

verse.note: This is almost certainly a symbolic name, not the woman’s own. Jezebel was the wife of Israel’s King Ahab, who promoted the worship of Baal and persecuted the Lord’s prophets (1 Kings 16–21). The name casts a prophet active in the Thyatira assembly as a new Jezebel leading God’s people into idolatry.

The Greek word is the ordinary one for a slave, a person who belongs to a master, not a hired servant. Most translations have “servants,” which softens this, though it reflects the fact that in the Septuagint the Lord’s “slaves” is also a title of honor for the prophets and for Israel. “Slaves” keeps the sense of belonging wholly to Christ.

text.q: I gave her time to turn back, but she is not willing to turn back from her sexual immorality.
Look, I am throwing her onto a sickbed, and those who commit adultery with her into great affliction, unless they turn back from her works;
and I will strike her children dead. Then all the assemblies will know that I am the one who searches minds and hearts, and I will give to each of you according to your works.
But to the rest of you in Thyatira, all who do not hold this teaching, who have not come to know the deep things of Satan, as they call them—to you I say: I am laying no other burden on you.
Only hold fast to what you have until I come.
To the one who conquers and keeps my works until the end I will give authority over the nations,

verse.note: The same Greek word is translated “Gentiles” elsewhere when it means the non-Jewish peoples. Verses 26–27 echo Psalm 2:8–9, where the peoples of the whole world are in view, so “nations” is used here.

text.q: to shepherd them with an iron rod, as clay pots are shattered,

verse.note: The verb means to tend a flock and was a common image for a king’s government; the “rod” is both a shepherd’s club and a scepter. The line echoes the Greek version of Psalm 2:9, which has “shepherd” where the Hebrew text as traditionally read has “break.” Most translations have “rule,” and some scholars think the verb here means simply to rule or even to devastate. “Shepherd” keeps the image a Greek reader met, and the same verb is used of the Lamb at 7:17.

text.q: just as I myself have received authority from my Father. And to that one I will give the morning star.
Let anyone who has an ear hear what the Spirit is saying to the assemblies.

“And to the angel of the assembly in Sardis write: These are the words of the one who has the seven spirits of God and the seven stars: I know your works—you have a name for being alive, yet you are dead.

verse.note: The Greek word means “messenger” and is the ordinary word for an angel. Most scholars take it here as a heavenly being who represents the community, since the word means “angel” everywhere else in Revelation. Others take it as a human messenger or leader of the community. The letter addresses this figure in the singular “you” but plainly speaks to the whole community.

The Greek word was the ordinary term for a civic gathering and, in the Greek Old Testament, for Israel assembled before God. “Church” is the near-universal rendering and is well understood, but it now suggests a building or an institution. “Assembly” is used throughout this translation so that the reader sees one word for one Greek word.

text.q: Wake up, and strengthen what remains, which was about to die, for I have not found your works complete before my God.
Remember, then, how you received and heard; keep it, and turn back. If you do not wake up, I will come like a thief, and you will never know at what hour I will come upon you.

verse.note: Most translations keep “repent” as the established term. In modern English that word centers on feeling sorry, whereas the Greek carries the prophets’ call to return to God, a change of direction in mind and conduct. “Turn back” is used for that reason.

text.q: But you have a few names in Sardis who have not soiled their garments, and they will walk with me in white, for they are worthy.

verse.note: “Names” here means persons, an idiom also found in Acts, and most modern versions translate “a few people.” The literal word is kept because the letter plays on it throughout: Sardis has a “name” for being alive (verse 1), a few “names” are unsoiled, and the conqueror’s “name” will not be erased but acknowledged (verse 5).

text.q: The one who conquers will be clothed like this in white garments, and I will never erase their name from the book of life, and I will acknowledge their name before my Father and before his angels.

verse.note: The verb is the ordinary Greek word for winning a battle, a contest or a lawsuit. The King James tradition has “overcometh,” and several modern versions keep “overcome,” while others use “conquer” in Revelation. The meaning is not disputed; “conquer” is chosen because it keeps the note of victory that “overcome” has largely lost.

text.q: Let anyone who has an ear hear what the Spirit is saying to the assemblies.
“And to the angel of the assembly in Philadelphia write: These are the words of the Holy One, the True One, who has the key of David, who opens and no one will shut, who shuts and no one opens:

verse.note: The wording echoes Isaiah 22:22, where the steward Eliakim is given the key of the house of David, so that what he opens no one shuts and what he shuts no one opens. The image is of sole authority to admit to or exclude from the royal household, here applied to the risen Christ and the kingdom.

text.q: I know your works—look, I have set before you an open door that no one is able to shut—that you have little power, and yet you kept my word and did not deny my name.

verse.note: The Greek conjunction can mean “that” or “because.” The translation follows the punctuation of the Greek edition, which treats the open door as a parenthesis, so that the clause states what Christ knows. The other reading is “I have set before you an open door … because you have little power and yet have kept my word.”

text.q: Look, I am giving some from the synagogue of Satan—those who say they are Jews and are not, but are lying—look, I will make them come and bow down before your feet, and they will know that I have loved you.

verse.note: The same phrase is used in the letter to Smyrna (2:9). It reflects a bitter local dispute between the Christ-believing assembly, many of whose members were themselves Jews, and the Jewish community in the city, over who truly belongs to God’s people. The language is polemic against particular opponents in a particular place, written by a Jewish author, and is not a statement about Jews as a people.

The verb names prostration in reverence, and what it signifies depends on who receives it. The King James Version has “worship before thy feet,” but the gesture here is made before human beings, so the physical act is translated, as in most modern versions. The scene reverses passages in Isaiah (such as 60:14) where the nations come and bow at Israel’s feet.

text.q: Because you kept my word about endurance, I also will keep you from the hour of testing that is about to come upon the whole world, to test those who live on the earth.

verse.note: The Greek is literally “the word of my endurance.” It may mean Christ’s command to endure, which is the reading followed here and in many versions, or the message about Christ’s own endurance in suffering. The grammar allows both.

The same verb “keep” is used for the Philadelphians’ loyalty and Christ’s response. Whether “keep from the hour” means being spared the ordeal altogether or being protected through it is disputed; a similar phrase in John 17:15 is often cited for protection within the trial. The translation leaves the question open, as the Greek does.

text.q: I am coming soon. Hold on to what you have, so that no one takes your crown.

I will make the one who conquers a pillar in the sanctuary of my God, and they will never again go outside; and I will write on them the name of my God and the name of the city of my God, the new Jerusalem, which comes down out of heaven from my God, and my own new name.

verse.note: Greek has two words that English Bibles usually both render “temple”: one for the whole complex with its courts, and this one for the building where God dwells. Most versions use “temple” here. “Sanctuary” is used throughout this translation to keep the two words distinct.

text.q: Let anyone who has an ear hear what the Spirit is saying to the assemblies.
“And to the angel of the assembly in Laodicea write: These are the words of the Amen, the faithful and true witness, the beginning of God’s creation:

verse.note: The Greek word can mean “beginning,” “origin” or “source,” or “ruler,” and translations are divided among them. “Beginning” is kept because Revelation uses the same word in the title “the beginning and the end” (21:6; 22:13). Many interpreters take the phrase to mean the one from whom creation originates, as in Colossians 1:15–18, and not the first thing created.

text.q: I know your works: you are neither cold nor hot. I wish you were cold or hot!

verse.note: Both cold and hot are good here; the wish is that Laodicea were one or the other. Many scholars see an allusion to the local water supply: nearby Hierapolis had hot springs and Colossae cold fresh water, while Laodicea’s piped water arrived tepid. The older reading that “cold” means open hostility to Christ is now generally doubted.

text.q: So, because you are lukewarm, and neither hot nor cold, I am about to vomit you out of my mouth.

verse.note: The Greek verb means to vomit. Most English versions soften it to “spit” or the older “spew.” The stronger word is kept because the image is of drink so nauseating that the body rejects it.

text.q: Because you say, ‘I am rich; I have grown rich and need nothing,’ and you do not know that you are the one who is wretched and pitiable and poor and blind and naked,

I advise you to buy from me gold refined by fire so that you may be rich, and white garments so that you may clothe yourself and the shame of your nakedness may not be exposed, and salve to rub on your eyes so that you may see.

verse.note: The three things offered answer Laodicea’s own sources of pride. The city was a wealthy banking center, known for garments of glossy black wool, and the region was associated with a medical school and an eye remedy. Christ offers true wealth, white garments and sight to a community that thinks it lacks nothing.

text.q: All those I love, I reprove and discipline. So be zealous and turn back.
Look, I am standing at the door and knocking. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will come in to them and dine with them, and they with me.
To the one who conquers I will grant to sit with me on my throne, just as I also conquered and sat down with my Father on his throne.
Let anyone who has an ear hear what the Spirit is saying to the assemblies.”

verse.text: After this I looked, and there was a door standing open in heaven, and the first voice, the one I had heard speaking with me like a trumpet, said, “Come up here, and I will show you what must take place.” After this

note.traditional: what must take place after this

verse.note: The Greek words for “after this” come next, and most translations attach them to the voice’s speech: “what must take place after this,” a phrase that echoes 1:19 and Daniel 2. The Greek edition translated here punctuates them as the opening of the next sentence, and the translation follows it. The earliest manuscripts had no punctuation, so either division is possible.

This points back to the trumpet-like voice of 1:10. There John turns toward the voice and sees the risen Jesus, so most interpreters take the speaker here to be Jesus, and the words are treated as his. Some think instead of an angel who guides John through the visions.

verse.text: I was at once in the Spirit, and there was a throne set in heaven, and on the throne someone was seated,
verse.note: The Greek has no article and could also be read “in spirit,” meaning a visionary state in which John’s own spirit is caught up. Most translations, as here, take it of God’s Spirit bringing the vision about, as at 1:10. The two readings are not far apart, since the experience is prophetic inspiration either way.

verse.text: and the one seated was like jasper and carnelian stone in appearance, and around the throne was a rainbow like emerald in appearance.

note.traditional: jasper and sardius (KJV “a jasper and a sardine stone”)

verse.note: Ancient gem names do not map exactly onto modern ones. The stone called jasper could be translucent and of various colors, and 21:11 describes it as clear as crystal. The second stone is a red gem, usually identified as carnelian. John describes the one on the throne only by radiance and color, never by form.

verse.text: Around the throne were twenty-four thrones, and on the thrones sat twenty-four elders, clothed in white garments, with golden crowns on their heads.
verse.note: The text does not say who the elders are, and their identity is disputed. Common proposals are a heavenly council of angelic beings, representatives of God’s people (twelve tribes and twelve apostles), or a counterpart to the twenty-four priestly divisions of 1 Chronicles 24. Their thrones, white garments and crowns mark them as honored and as sharing in rule.

verse.text: From the throne come flashes of lightning and rumblings and peals of thunder; and seven torches of fire are burning before the throne, which are the seven spirits of God,
verse.note: Many interpreters take this as a symbolic way of speaking of God’s one Spirit in its fullness, drawing on the seven lamps of Zechariah 4; some translations print “the sevenfold Spirit” in a footnote. Others understand seven chief angels who stand before God. The translation leaves the phrase as the Greek has it, in lowercase, without deciding.

verse.text: and before the throne there is something like a sea of glass, like crystal. And in the midst of the throne and around the throne are four living creatures, full of eyes in front and behind.

note.term: in the midst of the throne and around the throne
note.traditional: in the midst of the throne, and round about the throne

verse.note: The Greek is as hard to picture as the English. It may mean that the creatures stand close around the throne, one at the middle of each side, or that they are in some way part of the throne itself, as the cherubim are in Ezekiel’s vision. Translations vary: “around the throne, on each side of the throne,” or “in the center, around the throne.”

note.traditional: four beasts (KJV); four living creatures (most modern versions)

verse.note: The scene combines the four living creatures of Ezekiel 1, with their four faces and many eyes, and the six-winged seraphim of Isaiah 6, who cry “Holy, holy, holy.” The Greek word simply means a living being. It is a different word from the one used for the hostile “beast” later in the book.

verse.text: The first living creature is like a lion, the second living creature like an ox, the third living creature has a face like a human being’s, and the fourth living creature is like an eagle in flight.

And the four living creatures, each of them with six wings, are full of eyes all around and within, and they have no rest day or night, saying, “Holy, holy, holy is the Lord God, the Almighty, who was and who is and who is to come.”
And whenever the living creatures give glory and honor and thanks to the one seated on the throne, who lives forever and ever,
verse.note: The verbs in verses 9–10 are future in Greek: literally “whenever the living creatures will give … the elders will fall.” Most translators take this as describing what happens repeatedly, perhaps reflecting a Hebrew way of expressing customary action, and so use the English present. Some read it as a real future, pointing ahead to the worship described in the chapters that follow.

verse.text: the twenty-four elders fall down before the one seated on the throne and worship the one who lives forever and ever, and they cast their crowns before the throne, saying,

text.q: “You are worthy, our Lord and God, to receive the glory and the honor and the power, for you created all things, and because of your will they existed and were created.”

note.traditional: O Lord (KJV, following a different manuscript reading); our Lord and God

verse.note: The Roman writer Suetonius reports that the emperor Domitian liked to be addressed as “our lord and god.” Many scholars think the first hearers in Asia Minor would have heard this acclamation as a claim that such titles belong to God alone. Whether John intends a direct allusion is uncertain, since the pairing also has roots in the Greek Old Testament.

verse.text: And I saw in the right hand of the one seated on the throne a scroll written on the inside and on the back, sealed up with seven seals.

note.term: a scroll written on the inside and on the back

verse.note: The word means a written document, which in this period was normally a papyrus roll; the King James Version's “book” suggests a bound volume, and nearly all modern translations have “scroll.” Scrolls were usually written on the inner side only, so one written on both sides is unusually full, and the image echoes the scroll shown to Ezekiel (Ezekiel 2:9–10). Some punctuate differently: “written inside, and sealed on the back with seven seals.”

verse.text: And I saw a mighty angel proclaiming in a loud voice, “Who is worthy to open the scroll and break its seals?”
And no one in heaven or on earth or under the earth was able to open the scroll or to look into it.
And I was weeping bitterly because no one was found worthy to open the scroll or to look into it.
Then one of the elders said to me, “Do not weep. Look, the Lion from the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered, so that he can open the scroll and its seven seals.”

note.term: the Lion from the tribe of Judah, the Root of David

verse.note: Both titles come from Scripture read as promises of a royal deliverer: Judah is called a lion in Jacob's blessing (Genesis 49:9–10), and Isaiah speaks of a shoot and a root from the line of Jesse, David's father (Isaiah 11:1, 10). A first-century Jewish hearer would recognize these as titles of the Messiah descended from David.

note.traditional: has prevailed / has overcome / has triumphed

verse.note: The verb is the ordinary Greek word for winning a battle or contest. “Conquer” keeps the note of victory and ties this verse to the promises “to the one who conquers” in the letters to the seven churches; “overcome” can suggest merely getting past a difficulty. The meaning is not disputed, and several modern translations also use “conquer” in Revelation.

verse.text: And I saw, in the midst of the throne and of the four living creatures, and in the midst of the elders, a Lamb standing, as though slaughtered, with seven horns and seven eyes, which are the seven spirits of God sent out into all the earth.

note.term: in the midst of the throne and of the four living creatures, and in the midst of the elders

verse.note: The Greek repeats “in the midst of,” and the exact position is unclear. It may place the Lamb at the center of the throne, surrounded by the living creatures and the elders. It may instead reflect a Hebrew idiom meaning “between,” so that the Lamb stands between the throne with its living creatures on one side and the elders on the other. The rendering leaves both possibilities open.

The verb is the usual word for butchering an animal, especially in sacrifice, and for violent killing. “Slain” is traditional but has become a literary word that softens the picture; “slaughtered” keeps the image of a sacrificial animal, with echoes of the Passover lamb and of Isaiah 53:7. Some modern translations already use it.

In the Scriptures a horn is a standard image of strength and royal power, and seven is the number of completeness, so seven horns signify full power. The seven eyes recall Zechariah 4:10, where seven eyes of the Lord range over the whole earth. Whether “the seven spirits of God” means seven angelic spirits or is a symbolic way of speaking of God's Spirit in its fullness is disputed.

verse.text: And he came and took the scroll from the right hand of the one seated on the throne.

And when he had taken the scroll, the four living creatures and the twenty-four elders fell down before the Lamb, each holding a lyre and golden bowls full of incense, which are the prayers of the holy ones.
verse.note: The kithara was a hand-held stringed instrument of the lyre family, the standard instrument for accompanying song in the Greek world and, in the Greek Old Testament, in the temple. Most English versions say “harp,” which now suggests a large triangular instrument; “lyre” is closer to what a first-century reader would picture. Standard lexicons give both glosses.

The word refers to all members of God's people as those set apart for him, echoing the Greek Old Testament's language for Israel. “Saints” now suggests canonized individuals or people of exceptional virtue, which is not the sense. Many translations keep “saints”; others use “God's people.”

verse.text: And they sang a new song, saying, “You are worthy to take the scroll and to open its seals, because you were slaughtered, and with your blood you purchased for God those from every tribe and language and people and nation,

note.term: you purchased for God those from every tribe

verse.note: The Greek text translated here has no stated object for “purchased,” so “those” is supplied. Many later manuscripts add “us,” which the King James Version follows. Most editors consider the shorter reading, found in Codex Alexandrinus, to be original, since “us” fits poorly with “them” in the next verse.

This is the same Greek word that is translated “Gentiles” elsewhere in the New Testament when it refers to the non-Jewish peoples. Here, in a list covering all humanity, it has its general sense of a people or nation.

text.q: and you made them a kingdom and priests for our God, and they reign on the earth.”

verse.note: The manuscripts are divided between the present tense, “they reign,” printed in the Greek text translated here, and the future, “they will reign”; the two differ by a single letter. Many editors and most modern translations prefer the future. The King James Version's “we shall reign” and “made us kings and priests” follow later manuscripts that put the song in the first person.

verse.text: Then I looked, and I heard the voice of many angels around the throne and the living creatures and the elders, and their number was myriads of myriads and thousands of thousands,
saying in a loud voice, “Worthy is the Lamb who was slaughtered to receive power and wealth and wisdom and strength and honor and glory and blessing!”

And every creature that is in heaven and on earth and under the earth and on the sea, and all that is in them, I heard saying, “To the one seated on the throne and to the Lamb be blessing and honor and glory and dominion forever and ever!”
And the four living creatures kept saying, “Amen!” And the elders fell down and worshiped.
Then I watched as the Lamb opened one of the seven seals, and I heard one of the four living creatures say with a voice like thunder, “Come!”
verse.note: Many manuscripts add “and see” here and at the other three summonses, which makes the command an invitation to John; the King James Version follows that reading. Without the addition, the command is most naturally a summons to the horseman who then appears. The Greek verb can also mean “Go!”, and some translators render it that way.

verse.text: And I looked, and there was a white horse, and its rider had a bow. A crown was given to him, and he went out conquering and to conquer.
verse.note: The identity of the first rider is disputed. Some interpreters, ancient and modern, take him to be Christ or the advance of the gospel, pointing to the white horse of chapter 19. Most scholars today see him as military conquest, the first of four parallel disasters, with the bow suggesting a mounted archer. The crown is the victor’s wreath, and “conquer” is the same verb used in the promises to “the one who conquers” in the letters to the seven churches.

verse.text: When he opened the second seal, I heard the second living creature say, “Come!”
And out came another horse, fiery red. It was given to its rider to take peace from the earth, so that people would slaughter one another, and a great sword was given to him.
When he opened the third seal, I heard the third living creature say, “Come!” And I looked, and there was a black horse, and its rider had a pair of scales in his hand.

And I heard what seemed to be a voice in the midst of the four living creatures, saying, “A quart of wheat for a denarius, and three quarts of barley for a denarius—and do not harm the oil and the wine!”

note.term: A quart of wheat for a denarius
note.traditional: A measure of wheat for a penny

verse.note: The Greek measure, the choinix, held roughly a liter of grain, about one person’s daily ration, and a denarius was about a day’s wage for a laborer. These are famine prices, several times the normal rate: a day’s work buys only enough wheat for one person, or enough of the cheaper barley for a small household. Why the oil and wine are to be spared is debated; it may limit the famine’s severity or point to the bitter irony of luxuries surviving while bread fails.

verse.text: When he opened the fourth seal, I heard the voice of the fourth living creature say, “Come!”

And I looked, and there was a pale green horse. Its rider’s name was Death, and Hades followed along with him. They were given authority over a fourth of the earth, to kill with sword and with famine and with plague, and by the wild animals of the earth.
verse.note: The Greek word is the ordinary term for the green of plants (it is used of grass elsewhere in Revelation) and was also used for the yellowish-green pallor of the sick or dying. “Pale” alone loses the color; “pale green” keeps both the hue and the suggestion of a corpse. Several modern versions do the same.

The Greek word is the same as the rider’s name, “Death.” In the Greek Old Testament this word regularly translates the Hebrew term for pestilence, and the list here echoes Ezekiel 14:21, where God’s four judgments are sword, famine, wild beasts and pestilence. Most modern translations therefore have “plague” or “pestilence”; the King James Version keeps “death.”

verse.text: When he opened the fifth seal, I saw under the altar the souls of those who had been slaughtered because of the word of God and because of the testimony they held.
verse.note: In Israel’s sacrificial worship the blood of a victim, which was understood to carry its life, was poured out at the base of the altar. The picture presents those killed for their testimony as sacrifices, slaughtered like the Lamb himself; the same verb is used of both. Whether the altar of burnt offering or the incense altar is in view is debated.

verse.text: They cried out with a loud voice, “How long, Master, holy and true, until you judge and avenge our blood on those who live on the earth?”
verse.note: This is not the usual New Testament word for “Lord” but the term for the master of a household and owner of slaves, also used in prayer to God as absolute ruler. Many modern versions render it “Sovereign Lord”; the King James Version has “O Lord.” “Master” keeps it distinct from the ordinary word and preserves the link with “fellow slaves” in the next verse.

verse.text: And each of them was given a white robe, and they were told to rest a little while longer, until the number was made complete of their fellow slaves and brothers and sisters who were about to be killed as they themselves had been.
verse.note: The Greek word means someone who shares the condition of a slave under the same master. Most English versions soften it to “fellow servants.” Here it answers the address to God as “Master” in the previous verse. The “fellow slaves” and the “brothers and sisters” are probably one group described in two ways, though the Greek could also be read as two groups.

note.term: until the number was made complete

verse.note: The Greek says literally “until their fellow slaves … were completed.” Most translators take this to mean that a set number of martyrs must be reached, an idea found in other Jewish writings of the period. Some manuscripts have an active form, “until they complete,” which would mean until the others finish their course.

verse.text: And I watched when he opened the sixth seal, and there was a great earthquake; the sun became black as sackcloth made of hair, and the whole moon became like blood,

note.term: the sun became black as sackcloth made of hair
note.traditional: the sun became black as sackcloth of hair

verse.note: The signs in verses 12–14 draw on the prophets’ pictures of the day of the Lord: the sun darkened and the moon turned to blood in Joel 2:31, and the heavens rolled up like a scroll with their host falling like fruit from a fig tree in Isaiah 34:4. The cry to the mountains in verse 16 echoes Hosea 10:8. Sackcloth was coarse dark cloth, usually of goat hair, worn in mourning.

verse.text: and the stars of the sky fell to the earth, as a fig tree drops its unripe figs when shaken by a strong wind.
verse.note: The Greek word covers both the visible sky and God’s dwelling. Here and in verse 14 the stars and the visible vault overhead are meant, so “sky” is used, as in a number of modern versions; older versions have “heaven.”

verse.text: The sky was split apart like a scroll being rolled up, and every mountain and island was moved from its place.
verse.note: The verb means to separate or part. The picture may be of the sky splitting and curling back on itself like a scroll, or of the sky being removed altogether, as when a scroll is rolled up and put away; hence renderings such as “vanished” or “receded.” The Greek does not settle which is meant.

verse.text: Then the kings of the earth and the nobles and the commanders and the rich and the powerful, and every slave and free person, hid themselves in the caves and among the rocks of the mountains.
And they said to the mountains and the rocks, “Fall on us and hide us from the face of the one seated on the throne and from the wrath of the Lamb,

text.q: for the great day of their wrath has come, and who is able to stand?”

verse.note: The manuscripts are divided between “their wrath,” referring to both the one on the throne and the Lamb, and “his wrath.” The King James Version follows the latter; most modern editions and translations read “their,” judging that scribes were more likely to change the plural to match the preceding “wrath of the Lamb” than the reverse.

verse.text: After this I saw four angels standing at the four corners of the earth, holding back the four winds of the earth so that no wind would blow on the earth or on the sea or on any tree.

And I saw another angel coming up from the rising of the sun, holding the seal of the living God, and he cried out in a loud voice to the four angels who had been permitted to harm the earth and the sea,
saying, “Do not harm the earth or the sea or the trees until we have sealed the slaves of our God on their foreheads.”
verse.note: A seal was a stamp of ownership and protection, pressed on goods or documents to show whose they were. The scene recalls Ezekiel 9, where a mark is placed on the foreheads of the faithful in Jerusalem so that they are spared when judgment falls on the city.

The Greek word is the ordinary term for a slave, a person owned by a master, and the seal as a mark of ownership fits that sense. Most English versions have “servants,” partly because “slave” carries associations from modern history and partly because the Hebrew Scriptures use the equivalent term as a title of honor for those who belong to God. Both points are fair, but “servant” suggests a hired employee, which the word does not mean.

verse.text: And I heard the number of those who were sealed: one hundred forty-four thousand, sealed from every tribe of the sons of Israel:
verse.note: The number is twelve times twelve times a thousand, twelve thousand from each of twelve tribes. Interpreters disagree whether it refers to Jewish believers specifically or is a symbolic picture of the whole people of God. They also disagree whether the uncountable crowd of verse 9 is a second group or the same group seen from another angle; John hears the number and then sees the crowd.

verse.text: from the tribe of Judah twelve thousand were sealed, from the tribe of Reuben twelve thousand, from the tribe of Gad twelve thousand,
verse.note: The list does not match any tribal list in the Hebrew Scriptures. Judah, the tribe of the Messiah, stands first instead of Reuben the firstborn; Dan is missing; and Manasseh is listed alongside Joseph, his father, while Ephraim is not named. The reasons for the omission of Dan are uncertain, though ancient and modern interpreters have often linked it to that tribe’s association with idolatry.

verse.text: from the tribe of Asher twelve thousand, from the tribe of Naphtali twelve thousand, from the tribe of Manasseh twelve thousand,
from the tribe of Simeon twelve thousand, from the tribe of Levi twelve thousand, from the tribe of Issachar twelve thousand,
from the tribe of Zebulun twelve thousand, from the tribe of Joseph twelve thousand, from the tribe of Benjamin twelve thousand were sealed.

After these things I looked, and there was a great crowd that no one could count, from every nation and from all tribes and peoples and languages, standing before the throne and before the Lamb, clothed in white robes, with palm branches in their hands.
And they cry out in a loud voice, saying, “Salvation belongs to our God, who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb!”
verse.note: The Greek has no verb: literally “the salvation to our God … and to the Lamb.” The word covers rescue, deliverance and, in the Septuagint, sometimes victory; some translators render “Victory to our God.” The traditional rendering is kept, with the sense that deliverance is God’s work and is credited to him.

verse.text: And all the angels were standing around the throne and the elders and the four living creatures, and they fell on their faces before the throne and worshiped God,
saying, “Amen! Blessing and glory and wisdom and thanksgiving and honor and power and strength belong to our God forever and ever. Amen!”
Then one of the elders spoke up and said to me, “These people clothed in the white robes—who are they, and where have they come from?”
I said to him, “My lord, you know.” And he said to me, “These are the ones coming out of the great affliction; they have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.
verse.note: The word is the usual respectful address to a superior and is the same word used for “Lord” of God and Jesus. Here John addresses one of the elders, so it is not capitalized. Most versions have “Sir,” which is also accurate; “my lord” keeps the possessive pronoun the Greek has and the deference it expresses.

The Greek is a present participle. It may picture people still arriving as the vision unfolds, or it may simply describe the group without reference to time, as in the common rendering “those who have come out.” The following verbs, “washed” and “made white,” are past tense.

The Greek word was an ordinary term for oppressive hardship, the same one used for “great affliction” at Matthew 24:21 and Acts 7:11. “Tribulation” is now widely heard as the technical name of a specific end-time period, which says more than the word itself does. Whether the phrase here points to a single final crisis or to the whole course of the church’s suffering is debated; that is a question of what the phrase refers to, not of what the word means.

text.q: For this reason they are before the throne of God, and they serve him day and night in his sanctuary, and the one who sits on the throne will spread his tent over them.

verse.note: Greek has two words that English Bibles usually both translate “temple”: one for the whole complex with its courts, and this one for the building where God dwells. This translation renders the second as “sanctuary” throughout so that the distinction stays visible. Most versions have “temple” here, and standard lexicons allow either.

note.term: will spread his tent over them

verse.note: The verb means to pitch a tent or encamp, and here it takes a preposition meaning “over” or “upon,” not “among.” It evokes the tabernacle, the tent of God’s presence in the wilderness, and the promise that God would shelter his people. Older versions have “dwell among them” and several modern ones “shelter them”; the rendering here keeps both the tent image and the sense of covering.

text.q: They will hunger no more and thirst no more; the sun will not beat down on them, nor any scorching heat,

note.term: They will hunger no more and thirst no more

verse.note: Verses 16 and 17 are woven from the language of Isaiah, without being introduced as a quotation. Isaiah 49:10 promises the returning exiles that they will not hunger or thirst, that heat and sun will not strike them, and that they will be led to springs of water; Isaiah 25:8 promises that God will wipe away tears from all faces. Here the shepherd who leads them is the Lamb.

text.q: for the Lamb at the center of the throne will shepherd them and guide them to springs of the waters of life, and God will wipe away every tear from their eyes.”

verse.text: And when he opened the seventh seal, there was silence in heaven for about half an hour.
verse.note: The meaning of the silence is not explained and is disputed. Some connect it with the hush of awe before God’s judgment found in the prophets; others think heaven falls silent so that the prayers of verses 3–4 can be heard. Either way, it is a dramatic pause before the trumpets.

verse.text: And I saw the seven angels who stand before God, and seven trumpets were given to them.

note.term: the seven angels who stand before God

verse.note: The definite article suggests a group the readers already knew. Jewish tradition spoke of seven chief angels who stand in God’s presence (compare Tobit 12:15), and most interpreters think these are meant.

verse.text: Another angel came and stood at the altar, holding a golden censer, and he was given much incense to offer with the prayers of all the holy ones on the golden altar that is before the throne.
verse.note: The traditional rendering is “saints,” which many translations keep, while others use “God’s people.” “Saints” now suggests canonized individuals or people of exceptional virtue, whereas the Greek word is used of all believers as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint’s language for Israel.

The Greek has a bare dative, “to give to/for the prayers.” Most translations take it as “with the prayers,” the incense accompanying them as they rise. It can also be read as “on behalf of the prayers,” or as identifying the incense with the prayers, as in 5:8. The same construction recurs in verse 4.

verse.text: And the smoke of the incense, with the prayers of the holy ones, rose from the angel’s hand before God.
Then the angel took the censer and filled it with fire from the altar and threw it to the earth, and there came thunder and rumblings and flashes of lightning and an earthquake.
And the seven angels who had the seven trumpets prepared themselves to blow them.

The first blew his trumpet, and there came hail and fire mixed with blood, and it was thrown to the earth. A third of the earth was burned up, and a third of the trees were burned up, and all the green grass was burned up.

note.term: A third of the earth was burned up

verse.note: This clause is absent from the late manuscripts behind the King James Version, which therefore lacks it. The earliest and best manuscripts include it, and it was probably dropped by a copyist whose eye skipped between the three repeated endings “was burned up.”

verse.text: The second angel blew his trumpet, and something like a great mountain burning with fire was thrown into the sea. A third of the sea became blood,
a third of the creatures in the sea—those that had life—died, and a third of the ships were destroyed.
The third angel blew his trumpet, and a great star fell from the sky, blazing like a torch, and it fell on a third of the rivers and on the springs of water.
verse.note: The same Greek word covers both God’s dwelling and the visible sky. Older translations have “from heaven” here. A falling star belongs to the visible sky, so “sky” is used, while verse 1 keeps “heaven” for the scene at God’s throne.

verse.text: The name of the star is Wormwood. A third of the waters turned to wormwood, and many people died from the waters, because they had been made bitter.
verse.note: Wormwood is an intensely bitter plant. In the Hebrew Scriptures, wormwood and bitter or poisoned water are images of God’s judgment and of the bitterness of suffering (for example Jeremiah 9:15). The plant itself is not normally deadly, so the star’s name evokes that imagery of judgment and is not a botanical description.

verse.text: The fourth angel blew his trumpet, and a third of the sun was struck, and a third of the moon, and a third of the stars, so that a third of them would be darkened, and the day would not shine for a third of it, and the night likewise.

Then I looked, and I heard an eagle flying in midheaven, saying in a loud voice, “Woe, woe, woe to those who live on the earth, because of the remaining trumpet blasts of the three angels who are about to blow!”
verse.note: The late manuscripts behind the King James Version read “angel” here. The earliest and best manuscripts read “eagle,” and modern editions and translations follow them. The change to “angel” is probably a copyist’s attempt to supply a more expected speaker.

The Greek word is an astronomical term for the zenith, the highest point of the sky where the sun stands at noon. The eagle flies where everyone on earth can see and hear it. Some translations render it “directly overhead” or “high in the air.”

verse.text: Then the fifth angel blew his trumpet, and I saw a star that had fallen from heaven to the earth, and he was given the key to the shaft of the abyss.
verse.note: The Greek tense shows that John does not watch the star fall; he sees it already fallen. The star is treated as a personal being who receives a key and opens the shaft, in keeping with the Jewish habit of picturing angels as stars. Whether this figure is a fallen angel, an angel sent by God, or the same as the “angel of the abyss” in verse 11 is disputed.

The older tradition has “the bottomless pit,” which merges two Greek nouns into one image. The first word means a well or shaft; the second, in the Greek Old Testament, is the deep, and by this period was also used for the underworld prison of evil spirits. The picture is of a locked shaft leading down into that deep. Several modern versions also render it “shaft of the abyss.”

verse.text: He opened the shaft of the abyss, and smoke rose from the shaft like the smoke of a great furnace, and the sun and the air were darkened by the smoke from the shaft.
Out of the smoke locusts came onto the earth, and they were given power like the power that the scorpions of the earth have.
verse.note: The passive “was given” recurs through the chapter (verses 1, 3, and 5, where it is rendered “permitted”). In Jewish writing this is a reverent way of indicating that God is the one who grants or allows something. The destroyers act only within limits set from above.

verse.text: They were told not to harm the grass of the earth or any green plant or any tree, but only the people who do not have the seal of God on their foreheads.
They were not permitted to kill them, but only to torment them for five months; and their torment was like the torment of a scorpion when it stings a person.
verse.note: The reason for the figure is uncertain. A common suggestion is that it reflects the rough life span or season of natural locusts; others take it simply as a limited period. Either way the point is that the torment has a set end.

verse.text: In those days people will seek death and will never find it; they will long to die, and death flees from them.
The locusts looked like horses prepared for battle. On their heads were what seemed to be crowns like gold, and their faces were like human faces,
they had hair like women’s hair, and their teeth were like lions’ teeth,
they had breastplates like breastplates of iron, and the sound of their wings was like the sound of chariots with many horses rushing into battle.
They have tails like scorpions, and stingers, and in their tails is their power to harm people for five months.
They have as king over them the angel of the abyss; his name in Hebrew is Abaddon, and in Greek he has the name Apollyon.
verse.note: Abaddon is a Hebrew word meaning “destruction,” used in the Old Testament as a name for the realm of the dead alongside Sheol. Apollyon is a Greek word meaning “destroyer.” Some scholars hear in the Greek name a jab at the god Apollo, whose name was sometimes linked with the same verb, but this is not certain.

verse.text: The first woe has passed. Look, two more woes are still coming after this.
Then the sixth angel blew his trumpet, and I heard a voice from the horns of the golden altar that is before God,
verse.note: Many manuscripts read “the four horns,” and many English versions follow them. Other early witnesses lack “four,” and the Greek text translated here omits it. The horns are the projections at the corners of the altar, so the sense is unaffected.

verse.text: saying to the sixth angel, the one who had the trumpet, “Release the four angels who are bound at the great river Euphrates.”
verse.note: In the Old Testament the Euphrates marks the far boundary of the promised land, and the direction from which invading armies of Assyria and Babylon came. In John’s day it was also the eastern frontier of the Roman Empire, beyond which lay the Parthian cavalry that Rome feared.

verse.text: So the four angels were released, who had been kept ready for the hour and day and month and year, to kill a third of humankind.

note.term: the hour and day and month and year

verse.note: In Greek a single “the” governs all four nouns, so they name one appointed moment rather than four periods of time. The angels have been held for a precise point fixed in advance.

verse.text: The number of the cavalry troops was twice ten thousand times ten thousand; I heard their number.

note.term: twice ten thousand times ten thousand

verse.note: Literally “two myriads of myriads,” which works out to two hundred million. The myriad (ten thousand) was the largest number with its own name in Greek, and the expression echoes Old Testament language for countless hosts, so it may be meant as an unimaginably vast number, not an exact count.

verse.text: This is how I saw the horses in the vision, and those seated on them: they wore breastplates of fiery red, dark blue, and sulfur yellow. The heads of the horses were like lions’ heads, and out of their mouths came fire and smoke and sulfur.

note.term: fiery red, dark blue, and sulfur yellow
note.traditional: of fire, and of jacinth, and brimstone

verse.note: The Greek has three adjectives: “fiery,” “hyacinth-like,” and “sulfurous.” They are usually understood as colors, with “hyacinth” denoting a dark blue or violet like smoke, so that the breastplates match the fire, smoke, and sulfur coming from the horses’ mouths. They could instead describe material or appearance. The Greek also leaves open whether the breastplates belong to the riders alone or to horses and riders together.

verse.text: By these three plagues a third of humankind was killed—by the fire and the smoke and the sulfur that came out of their mouths.
For the power of the horses is in their mouths and in their tails; for their tails are like snakes, with heads, and with them they do harm.

The rest of humankind, those who were not killed by these plagues, still did not turn back from the works of their hands, so as to stop worshiping demons and the idols of gold and silver and bronze and stone and wood, which can neither see nor hear nor walk,
verse.note: Most translations have “repent,” an established term that readers are expected to understand as including a change of life. In current English, however, “repent” centers on feeling sorry. The Greek word carries the prophets’ call to return to God, a change of direction in mind and conduct, and “turn back” is used here to keep that sense.

verse.text: and they did not turn back from their murders or their sorceries or their sexual immorality or their thefts.
verse.note: The Greek word means drugs, potions, or poisons, and by extension the charms and spells that used them. Most translations take it here as magical practice in general. Coming directly after “murders,” it could also be read as “poisonings.” Some manuscripts have the closely related abstract noun for sorcery instead.

verse.text: Then I saw another mighty angel coming down from heaven, wrapped in a cloud, with the rainbow over his head; his face was like the sun, and his legs were like pillars of fire.
verse.note: The Greek word normally means “foot,” and it is translated that way in verse 2, where the angel plants one on the sea and one on the land. Here the comparison to pillars shows that the whole limb is in view, a wider use the word allows, so most modern versions say “legs.” Older versions keep “feet.”

verse.text: He held in his hand a little scroll that lay open. He set his right foot on the sea and his left on the land,
and he cried out with a loud voice, as a lion roars. And when he cried out, the seven thunders spoke in their own voices.
verse.note: The Greek has the definite article, as if these thunders were already known to the reader, though the book has not mentioned them before. Many interpreters see an echo of Psalm 29, where “the voice of the Lord” thunders seven times. That link is plausible but not certain.

verse.text: And when the seven thunders had spoken, I was about to write, but I heard a voice from heaven saying, “Seal up what the seven thunders said, and do not write it down.”
Then the angel whom I had seen standing on the sea and on the land raised his right hand to heaven
and swore by the one who lives forever and ever, who created heaven and what is in it, the earth and what is in it, and the sea and what is in it: “There will be no more delay,

note.term: There will be no more delay
note.traditional: there should be time no longer

verse.note: The Greek is literally “time will no longer be.” Older versions took this to mean that time itself would cease. Most scholars now read the word as “an interval” or “delay,” because the next clause says what happens instead: God’s purpose is completed without further waiting. The scene, with a hand raised to heaven and an oath by the one who lives forever, echoes Daniel 12:7, where the question is how long it will be until the end.

text.q: but in the days of the sound of the seventh angel, when he is about to blow his trumpet, the secret of God will be brought to completion, just as he announced the good news to his own slaves the prophets.”

verse.note: Most English versions keep “mystery,” treating it as a technical term for a truth once hidden and now revealed. In Jewish Greek of the period the word was the ordinary term for a secret, especially God’s hidden plan that only he can disclose. English “mystery” now suggests a puzzle or something unknowable, which is not the point here.

Most versions say only that God “announced” or “declared” this to the prophets. The verb is the one elsewhere translated “preach the gospel,” an ordinary word for bringing good news. The translation keeps that sense visible: the completion of God’s secret plan is presented as good news.

Nearly all English versions have “his servants the prophets,” a phrase familiar from the Old Testament. The Greek word is the ordinary term for a slave, someone who belongs to a master, not a hired servant. In Jewish usage, to be called God’s slave was a title of honor, borne by Moses and the prophets.

verse.text: Then the voice that I had heard from heaven spoke with me again and said, “Go, take the scroll that lies open in the hand of the angel who is standing on the sea and on the land.”
So I went to the angel and told him to give me the little scroll. And he said to me, “Take it and eat it up. It will make your stomach bitter, but in your mouth it will be sweet as honey.”
verse.note: The scene is modeled on the call of the prophet Ezekiel (Ezekiel 2:8–3:3), who is told to eat a scroll of God’s words and finds it sweet as honey in his mouth. The bitterness in the stomach is John’s own addition. It is usually taken to reflect the painful content of the message he must deliver.

verse.text: So I took the little scroll from the angel’s hand and ate it up, and in my mouth it was sweet as honey; but when I had eaten it, my stomach was made bitter.
Then I was told, “You must prophesy again about many peoples and nations and languages and kings.”
verse.note: The preposition can mean “about,” “against,” or “in the presence of.” Older versions have “before,” and some interpreters prefer “against,” since the prophecies that follow are largely judgments. “About” is the most common modern rendering and leaves the tone open.

This is the same Greek word that is translated “Gentiles” elsewhere in the New Testament, where it means the non-Jewish peoples. In Revelation’s repeated lists of peoples, nations, and languages, the scope is all the peoples of the world, so “nations” is used.

verse.text: Then I was given a reed like a rod, and I was told, “Get up and measure the sanctuary of God and the altar and those who worship in it.
verse.note: Greek has one word for the whole temple complex with its courts and another, used here, for the building where God dwells. Most English versions render both as “temple.” The distinction matters in this passage, because the outer court in verse 2 lies outside what is measured.

note.traditional: and the angel stood, saying (KJV); and I was told (most modern versions)

verse.note: The Greek has only a participle, “saying,” with no stated speaker. The voice goes on to say “my two witnesses” in verse 3, which suggests God or Christ, or an angel speaking for them. Where the speech ends is also uncertain; it is closed here after verse 3, as in most versions, though some extend it further.

text.q: But leave out the court outside the sanctuary and do not measure it, because it has been given to the Gentiles, and they will trample the holy city for forty-two months.

verse.note: The same Greek word is translated “nations” in verses 9 and 18. It means peoples in general and, in the plural, often the non-Jewish peoples specifically. “Gentiles” is used here because the image is of the temple’s outer court and the holy city handed over to foreigners; “nations” is equally possible.

Forty-two months, the one thousand two hundred sixty days of verse 3, and three and a half years are the same span. It echoes the “time, times, and half a time” of Daniel (7:25; 12:7), a limited period in which God’s people are oppressed. The three and a half days of verses 9 and 11 mirror the figure on a small scale.

text.q: And I will grant it to my two witnesses to prophesy for one thousand two hundred sixty days, clothed in sackcloth.”

verse.text: These are the two olive trees and the two lampstands that stand before the Lord of the earth.

note.term: the two olive trees and the two lampstands

verse.note: The image comes from Zechariah 4, where two olive trees stand beside a golden lampstand and are identified as the two anointed ones who stand by the Lord of the whole earth. In Zechariah’s setting these are usually understood as the governor Zerubbabel and the high priest Joshua.

verse.text: And if anyone wants to harm them, fire comes out of their mouth and devours their enemies; if anyone should want to harm them, this is how that person must be killed.

They have the authority to shut the sky, so that no rain may fall during the days of their prophesying, and they have authority over the waters, to turn them into blood, and to strike the earth with every kind of plague as often as they wish.
verse.note: The powers described recall Elijah, who announced a drought and called down fire (1 Kings 17; 2 Kings 1), and Moses, who turned water into blood and struck Egypt with plagues (Exodus 7–11). Whether the two witnesses are meant as these figures returned, as other individuals, or as a symbol of the witnessing church is disputed.

verse.text: And when they have finished their testimony, the beast that comes up out of the abyss will make war on them and conquer them and kill them.
verse.note: The Greek verb is the ordinary word for winning a victory in battle or in a contest. “Overcome” in modern English can suggest merely getting past a difficulty, and it hides the link with the promises to “the one who conquers” elsewhere in Revelation. The meaning is not disputed; several modern versions also use “conquer” here.

verse.text: And their corpses will lie on the main street of the great city, which is spiritually called Sodom and Egypt, where their Lord also was crucified.

note.traditional: spiritually (KJV); symbolically, figuratively or prophetically (modern versions)

verse.note: The adverb signals that the names Sodom and Egypt are not literal, but belong to the Spirit’s way of seeing the city; modern versions paraphrase as “symbolically” or “prophetically.” The reference to the crucifixion points to Jerusalem, yet “the great city” elsewhere in Revelation is Babylon. Many interpreters therefore take it as a composite image of the world city opposed to God.

verse.text: And some from among the peoples and tribes and languages and nations look at their corpses for three and a half days, and they do not allow their corpses to be placed in a tomb.
verse.note: The Greek shifts here from future verbs to the present tense (“look,” “do not allow,” “rejoice,” “celebrate”) and then back to the future (“will send”). Most versions smooth everything into the future. The shifts are kept here because they are in the Greek, where the vision slips between prediction and vivid description.

verse.text: And those who live on the earth rejoice over them and celebrate, and they will send gifts to one another, because these two prophets tormented those who live on the earth.
And after the three and a half days a breath of life from God entered them, and they stood on their feet, and great fear fell on those who were watching them.

note.traditional: the Spirit of life (KJV); a breath of life (ESV, NRSV)

verse.note: The Greek word means both “breath” and “spirit.” The wording echoes Ezekiel 37, where breath enters the slain and they stand on their feet, so “breath” is used here. “A spirit of life from God” is also possible.

verse.text: And they heard a loud voice from heaven saying to them, “Come up here!” And they went up to heaven in the cloud, and their enemies watched them.

And in that hour there was a great earthquake, and a tenth of the city fell, and seven thousand people were killed in the earthquake, and the rest became terrified and gave glory to the God of heaven.
The second woe has passed. Look, the third woe is coming soon.

Then the seventh angel blew his trumpet, and there were loud voices in heaven, saying, “The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and he will reign forever and ever.”
And the twenty-four elders who sit before God on their thrones fell on their faces and worshiped God,
saying, “We give you thanks, Lord God, the Almighty, who is and who was, because you have taken your great power and begun to reign.

note.traditional: which art, and wast, and art to come (KJV)

verse.note: Some later manuscripts add “and who is to come,” matching the fuller title in 1:4, 1:8 and 4:8, and the King James Version follows them. The earliest and best witnesses lack the phrase. Its absence fits the context: the hymn celebrates that God has now come to reign.

text.q: The nations grew angry, and your anger has come, and the time for the dead to be judged, and for giving the reward to your slaves the prophets and to the holy ones and to those who fear your name, the small and the great, and for destroying those who destroy the earth.”

note.term: The nations grew angry, and your anger has come
note.traditional: The nations raged (or were angry), and your wrath has come

verse.note: The Greek uses a verb and a noun from the same root, setting the nations’ anger against God’s. Most versions use “wrath” for God’s anger and so lose the echo. The line recalls Psalm 2, where the nations rage against the Lord and his anointed, the same psalm that lies behind “our Lord and his Christ” in verse 15.

The Greek word is the ordinary term for a slave, someone who belongs to a master, and not for a hired servant. “Your servants the prophets” is a set Old Testament phrase and most versions keep “servants.” In that phrase the word is a title of honor for those wholly at God’s disposal, but a first-century reader still heard the word for a slave.

“Saints” now suggests canonized individuals or people of exceptional virtue. The Greek word is used of all members of the community as people set apart for God, echoing the Old Testament’s language for Israel. Many versions keep “saints”; others use “God’s people” or “his holy people.”

verse.text: Then the sanctuary of God in heaven was opened, and the ark of his covenant was seen in his sanctuary, and there came flashes of lightning and rumblings and peals of thunder and an earthquake and heavy hail.
And a great sign appeared in heaven: a woman clothed with the sun, with the moon under her feet, and on her head a crown of twelve stars.
verse.note: The Greek word means both “heaven” and “sky”, and a first-century reader would not have needed to choose. The signs here could equally be read as appearing “in the sky”, where sun, moon and stars are. “Heaven” is kept because the scene continues from the heavenly temple of the preceding verse and leads into the war in heaven in verse 7; in verse 4 the same word is rendered “sky”.

verse.text: She was pregnant, and she was crying out in labor pains, in agony to give birth.
And another sign appeared in heaven: look, a great red dragon with seven heads and ten horns, and on his heads seven diadems.
verse.note: In Greek this word meant a huge serpent, not the winged, fire-breathing creature of later European legend. The Greek Old Testament uses it for the sea monsters, such as Leviathan, that stand for chaos and for hostile empires like Egypt and Babylon. That is why verse 9 can call the same figure “the ancient serpent” without changing the image.

verse.text: His tail dragged down a third of the stars of the sky and threw them to the earth. And the dragon stood in front of the woman who was about to give birth, so that when she bore her child he might devour it.
And she gave birth to a son, a male child, who is going to shepherd all the nations with an iron rod. And her child was snatched up to God and to his throne.
verse.note: The Greek verb is the ordinary word for tending a flock, and was a common image for a king’s government. The phrase echoes Psalm 2:9 in its Greek form, where the Hebrew is usually read as “break”. Most translations render “rule”, and many scholars hold that with an iron rod the sense is stern or even destructive. “Shepherd” keeps the image a Greek reader would have heard.

The same Greek word is rendered “Gentiles” elsewhere in this translation where it means the non-Jewish peoples as distinct from Israel. Here, as generally in Revelation, the scope is all the peoples of the world, so “nations” is used.

verse.text: And the woman fled into the wilderness, where she has a place prepared by God, so that there she would be nourished for one thousand two hundred sixty days.

note.term: one thousand two hundred sixty days
note.traditional: a thousand two hundred and threescore days

verse.note: This is the same period as the “time and times and half a time” of verse 14 (three and a half years) and the forty-two months mentioned elsewhere in Revelation.
