The figure comes from Daniel 7:25 and 12:7, where it marks a limited period during which God’s people are oppressed. How the period should be understood is disputed among interpreters.

verse.text: And war broke out in heaven: Michael and his angels waged war on the dragon. The dragon waged war, and his angels with him,
but he was not strong enough, and no place was found for them in heaven any longer.

And the great dragon was thrown down, the ancient serpent, the one called Devil and Satan, the one who leads the whole world astray—he was thrown down to the earth, and his angels were thrown down with him.

note.term: the ancient serpent, the one called Devil and Satan
note.traditional: that old serpent, called the Devil, and Satan

verse.note: “Satan” is a Hebrew word meaning adversary or accuser, and the Greek word behind “Devil” means slanderer and is the Greek Old Testament’s usual translation of it. Both names prepare for the title “the accuser” in verse 10. “The ancient serpent” points back to the serpent of Genesis 3, whose enmity with the woman and her offspring (Genesis 3:15) is echoed in verse 17.

verse.text: And I heard a loud voice in heaven saying, “Now the salvation and the power and the kingdom of our God and the authority of his Christ have come, because the accuser of our brothers and sisters has been thrown down, the one who accuses them before our God day and night.
verse.note: The Greek plural was the normal way to address or refer to a mixed group of fellow believers, women as well as men. “Brothers” alone now suggests men only, so the fuller phrase is used. Several modern translations do the same; others keep “brothers”.

text.q: And they conquered him because of the blood of the Lamb and because of the word of their testimony, and they did not love their lives even to the point of death.

verse.note: The Greek verb is the ordinary word for winning a battle, a contest or a lawsuit. “Conquer” keeps the note of victory and the link with the promises “to the one who conquers” earlier in Revelation; “overcome” in modern English can suggest merely getting past a difficulty. The meaning is not disputed, and some major translations also use “conquer” here.

note.traditional: by the blood of the Lamb

verse.note: The Greek construction normally gives the ground or reason for something rather than the instrument, so “because of” is the more exact rendering: the Lamb’s death and their testimony are the basis of the victory. Most translations have “by”, and some scholars think the distinction had weakened by this period. A few translations render as here.

text.q: Therefore rejoice, you heavens and you who dwell in them! Woe to the earth and the sea, because the devil has come down to you in great fury, knowing that he has only a short time.”

verse.text: And when the dragon saw that he had been thrown down to the earth, he pursued the woman who had given birth to the male child.

But the woman was given the two wings of the great eagle, so that she might fly into the wilderness to her place, where she is nourished for a time and times and half a time, away from the presence of the serpent.
Then the serpent spewed water like a river from his mouth after the woman, so that the river would sweep her away.
But the earth helped the woman: the earth opened its mouth and swallowed the river that the dragon had spewed from his mouth.
And the dragon was enraged at the woman and went off to make war on the rest of her offspring, those who keep the commandments of God and hold the testimony of Jesus.
verse.note: The Greek can mean either the testimony that Jesus himself gave, which his followers hold fast, or their testimony about Jesus. Scholars are divided, and the translation leaves the phrase as open as the Greek. Some later manuscripts add “Christ”, which is why older English versions include it.

verse.text: And he stood on the sand of the sea.

note.traditional: And I stood upon the sand of the sea

verse.note: The earliest and best manuscripts read “he stood”, meaning the dragon, who takes his place on the shore as the beast rises from the sea in the next chapter. Many later manuscripts read “I stood”, making John the subject, and the King James Version follows them. Editions also differ on numbering: this sentence is variously counted as 12:18, the end of 12:17, or the beginning of 13:1.

verse.text: And I saw a beast rising out of the sea, with ten horns and seven heads, and on its horns ten diadems, and on its heads blasphemous names.
And the beast that I saw was like a leopard, and its feet were like a bear’s, and its mouth was like a lion’s mouth. And the dragon gave it his power and his throne and great authority.
verse.note: The description draws on Daniel 7, where four beasts rise from the sea in turn: one like a lion, one like a bear, one like a leopard, and a fourth with ten horns. Here their features are combined in a single beast. In Daniel the beasts stand for successive empires, and a first-century reader would have heard this one as an image of imperial power.

verse.text: And one of its heads looked as though it had been slaughtered to death, yet its mortal wound was healed. And the whole earth marveled and followed the beast,

note.traditional: wounded to death; seemed to have a mortal wound

verse.note: Most translations soften this to “wounded.” The Greek uses the same verb, in the same form, that describes the Lamb “as though slaughtered” in 5:6 and “slaughtered” in verse 8. Rendering it the same way lets the reader see that the beast is presented as a counterfeit of the Lamb.

verse.text: and they worshiped the dragon because he had given the authority to the beast, and they worshiped the beast, saying, “Who is like the beast, and who can wage war against it?”
And it was given a mouth speaking boastful words and blasphemies, and it was given authority to act for forty-two months.
verse.note: The same passive verb recurs through the chapter, rendered “was given” with a noun and “was allowed” with a verb (verses 7, 14, 15). No giver is named. Most interpreters take the repeated passive to mean that the beast acts only within limits set by God, though in verses 2 and 4 the dragon is the one who gives the beast its authority.

verse.text: And it opened its mouth in blasphemies against God, to blaspheme his name and his dwelling, that is, those who dwell in heaven.
verse.note: The Greek word means “tent” and recalls Israel’s tent-sanctuary in the wilderness. It is rendered “dwelling” here because the verb that follows, “dwell,” comes from the same root, and the wordplay would otherwise be lost. Some manuscripts add “and” before “those who dwell in heaven,” making them a third object; the text translated here identifies God’s dwelling with those heavenly dwellers.

verse.text: And it was allowed to make war on the holy ones and to conquer them, and it was given authority over every tribe and people and language and nation.
verse.note: The traditional “saints” now suggests canonized individuals or people of exceptional virtue. The Greek term is used of all members of the community as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint’s language for Israel. Many translations keep “saints”; others use “God’s people.”

The Greek verb is the ordinary word for winning a victory in battle. It is the same verb used for the promises “to the one who conquers” in chapters 2 and 3. Older versions use “overcome”; several modern versions use “conquer” in Revelation, and the meaning is not disputed.

The Greek word here is the same one translated “Gentiles” elsewhere in the New Testament. It means a people or nation, and in the plural often the non-Jewish peoples. In this fourfold list the sense is plainly all the peoples of the world.

verse.text: And all who live on the earth will worship it, everyone whose name has not been written in the book of life of the Lamb who was slaughtered from the foundation of the world.

note.term: slaughtered from the foundation of the world

verse.note: The translation follows the Greek word order, in which “from the foundation of the world” stands directly after “slaughtered.” The phrase can instead be attached to “written,” giving “whose name has not been written from the foundation of the world in the book of life of the Lamb who was slaughtered.” The closely parallel wording of 17:8 supports that alternative. Translations and commentators are divided.

verse.text: If anyone has an ear, let them hear.
If anyone is for captivity, into captivity they go. If anyone is to be killed by the sword, by the sword they are to be killed. Here is the endurance and the faith of the holy ones.

note.term: If anyone is to be killed by the sword, by the sword they are to be killed

verse.note: The manuscripts differ considerably here. The text translated, which follows Codex Alexandrinus, speaks of the fate believers must accept and echoes Jeremiah 15:2. Many other manuscripts read “if anyone kills with the sword, with the sword he must be killed,” a warning of retribution, and several well-known translations follow that reading.

verse.text: And I saw another beast rising out of the earth, and it had two horns like a lamb, and it spoke like a dragon.
And it exercises all the authority of the first beast in its sight. And it makes the earth and those who live in it worship the first beast, whose mortal wound was healed.
And it performs great signs, even making fire come down from heaven to the earth in the sight of people.

And it deceives those who live on the earth because of the signs it was allowed to perform in the sight of the beast, telling those who live on the earth to make an image for the beast that has the wound of the sword and yet lived.
And it was allowed to give breath to the image of the beast, so that the image of the beast would even speak and would cause all who do not worship the image of the beast to be killed.
verse.note: The Greek word means both “breath” and “spirit,” and either is possible; the point is that the image is made to seem alive. It is also unclear whether the one who causes the killing is the image or the second beast. The Greek grammar slightly favors the image.

verse.text: And it causes everyone, the small and the great, the rich and the poor, the free and the slaves, to be given a mark on their right hand or on their forehead,
verse.note: The Greek word was used for a stamped, engraved, or branded impression, including the imprint on coins and official seals. The mark on the hand or forehead parodies the seal placed on the foreheads of God’s servants in 7:3. Whether the author had a specific practice in view is uncertain.

verse.text: so that no one can buy or sell except the one who has the mark, the name of the beast or the number of its name.
Here is wisdom. Let the one who has understanding calculate the number of the beast, for it is the number of a person, and its number is six hundred sixty-six.
verse.note: The phrase can mean the number of a particular individual, whose name adds up to the figure given, or simply “a human number,” one reckoned in the ordinary human way (compare 21:17). Most interpreters take it as pointing to an individual. Traditional versions have “the number of a man.”

In Greek and Hebrew, letters also served as numerals, so any name had a numerical total. The most widely held view is that the number comes from “Nero Caesar” written in Hebrew letters, though this is not certain and other solutions have been proposed. A few early manuscripts read six hundred sixteen, a variant already known in the second century; it fits a different spelling of the same name.

verse.text: Then I looked, and there was the Lamb, standing on Mount Zion, and with him one hundred forty-four thousand who had his name and his Father’s name written on their foreheads.
And I heard a sound from heaven like the sound of many waters and like the sound of loud thunder, and the sound I heard was like harpists playing on their harps.

And they sing something like a new song before the throne and before the four living creatures and the elders, and no one could learn the song except the one hundred forty-four thousand, who had been bought from the earth.
verse.note: The verb is the ordinary word for buying in a market, the same one used for buying and selling in 13:17. Most translations have “redeemed” here, though some have “purchased.” The image is of a purchase that transfers ownership to God, as in 5:9, and “redeemed” belongs more properly to a different Greek word group.

verse.text: These are the ones who have not defiled themselves with women, for they are virgins. These are the ones who follow the Lamb wherever he goes. These were bought from among humankind as firstfruits for God and for the Lamb,
verse.note: Taken literally, this describes a company of celibate men. Most interpreters read it figuratively: Israel’s soldiers abstained from sex while on campaign, and the prophets describe idolatry as sexual unfaithfulness, so the picture is of a people who have kept themselves from the worship of the beast. Which reading is intended remains disputed.

verse.text: and in their mouth no lie was found; they are without blemish.
verse.note: In the Septuagint this is the regular term for a sacrificial animal free of any defect. Coming directly after “firstfruits,” another offering term, the sacrificial sense is probably intended. Most translations have “blameless,” which the word can also mean when used of moral character.

verse.text: Then I saw another angel flying high overhead, with eternal good news to announce to those who live on the earth, to every nation and tribe and language and people,
verse.note: The Greek word was an ordinary term for a public announcement of good news, and “gospel” now sounds like a religious term or a book title. The Greek here has no article, and the announcement that follows is a summons to fear and worship the Creator because his judgment has arrived. Many modern translations alternate between “gospel” and “good news.”

This is the same Greek word that this translation renders “Gentiles” where it refers to the non-Jewish peoples. In Revelation’s lists of nation, tribe, language and people, and in “all the nations” in verse 8, the peoples of the whole world are meant, so “nation” is used.

verse.text: saying in a loud voice, “Fear God and give him glory, because the hour of his judgment has come. Worship the one who made heaven and earth, the sea and the springs of water.”
And another angel, a second, followed, saying, “Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great, who has made all the nations drink the wine of the passion of her sexual immorality.”
verse.note: The cry echoes Isaiah 21:9. Babylon, the empire that destroyed Jerusalem and its temple in the sixth century BC, serves in Revelation as the name of a great oppressing city. Most scholars identify it with Rome.

The Greek word is the same one rendered “fury” in verses 10 and 19, and it can mean either intense passion or anger. Many translations take it as “passion” here; others render “wrath,” so that the wine Babylon serves the nations already carries God’s anger. The echo between Babylon’s wine and God’s wine in verse 10 is almost certainly deliberate. The sexual immorality is a prophetic figure for the idolatry and corrupting alliances into which the city draws the nations.

verse.text: And another angel, a third, followed them, saying in a loud voice, “If anyone worships the beast and its image and receives a mark on the forehead or on the hand,

text.q: that person too will drink the wine of God’s fury, poured undiluted into the cup of his wrath, and will be tormented with fire and sulfur before holy angels and before the Lamb.

verse.note: The Greek is literally “mixed unmixed.” Wine was normally diluted with water before drinking, and the verb for mixing had come to mean simply preparing or pouring wine, so the phrase means wine served at full strength. The cup of God’s wrath is an image from the prophets, for example Jeremiah 25:15.

text.q: And the smoke of their torment rises forever and ever, and they have no rest day or night, those who worship the beast and its image, and anyone who receives the mark of its name.”

verse.text: This calls for the endurance of the holy ones, those who keep the commandments of God and their faith in Jesus.
verse.note: “Saints” now suggests canonized individuals or people of exceptional virtue. The Greek word is used of all members of the community as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint’s language for Israel. Many translations keep “saints”; others use “God’s people.”

The Greek is literally “the faith of Jesus.” It can mean faith in Jesus, which most translations adopt, or Jesus’s own faithfulness, or the faith that comes from Jesus. The word “their” is supplied for the sake of English.

verse.text: And I heard a voice from heaven saying, “Write: Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord from now on.” “Yes,” says the Spirit, “so that they may rest from their labors, for their deeds follow along with them.”
Then I looked, and there was a white cloud, and seated on the cloud was one like a son of man, with a golden crown on his head and a sharp sickle in his hand.

note.term: one like a son of man
note.traditional: one like unto the Son of man

verse.note: The phrase echoes Daniel 7:13, where a human-looking figure comes with the clouds of heaven; the same wording describes the risen Jesus in 1:13. Most interpreters identify the figure here as Christ. A minority take him to be an angel, because “another angel” follows and gives him the command to reap. The Greek lacks the article found in the Gospel title “the Son of Man,” so the phrase is left in lowercase.

verse.text: And another angel came out of the sanctuary, crying out in a loud voice to the one seated on the cloud, “Put in your sickle and reap, because the hour to reap has come, for the harvest of the earth is ripe.”
verse.note: Greek has two words that English Bibles usually both render “temple”: one for the whole complex with its courts, and this one for the building where God dwells. “Sanctuary” keeps the distinction; here it is the heavenly dwelling of God from which the angels come. Most translations use “temple” for both words.

verse.text: So the one seated on the cloud swung his sickle over the earth, and the earth was reaped.
Then another angel came out of the sanctuary in heaven, and he too had a sharp sickle.

And another angel, the one who has authority over the fire, came out from the altar, and he called in a loud voice to the one who had the sharp sickle, “Put in your sharp sickle and gather the clusters from the vine of the earth, because its grapes are fully ripe.”
So the angel swung his sickle over the earth and gathered the clusters from the vine of the earth, and threw them into the great winepress of God’s fury.
And the winepress was trodden outside the city, and blood flowed from the winepress as high as the horses’ bridles for a distance of one thousand six hundred stadia.

note.traditional: a thousand and six hundred furlongs

verse.note: A stadion was about 185 meters, so the distance is roughly 300 kilometers or 180 miles. The figure is kept rather than converted because it is probably symbolic: sixteen hundred is four squared times ten squared, and four is Revelation’s number for the whole earth. Some translations convert it to “two hundred miles.”

verse.text: Then I saw another sign in heaven, great and marvelous: seven angels with seven plagues, the last ones, because with them the fury of God is completed.
verse.note: Revelation uses two Greek words for God’s anger, sometimes side by side (16:19; 19:15), and most English versions render both as “wrath.” The word here is the more passionate of the two, used in the period for an outburst of anger. “Fury” keeps it distinct from the other word, which is rendered “wrath.”

verse.text: And I saw what looked like a sea of glass mixed with fire, and those who had conquered the beast and its image and the number of its name, standing on the sea of glass, holding harps of God.
verse.note: The verb is the ordinary Greek word for winning a battle or a contest, and “conquer” keeps that note of victory better than “overcome.” The construction is unusual: literally “those conquering out of the beast,” probably meaning those who came out of the struggle with the beast as victors. The meaning is not disputed, and several modern versions also use “conquer” in Revelation.

note.term: standing on the sea of glass
note.traditional: standing beside the sea of glass

verse.note: The preposition can mean either “on” or “at, beside.” Many modern versions choose “beside,” which strengthens the echo of Israel standing on the shore of the sea in Exodus 14–15. “On” is the more usual sense of the construction in Revelation and suits a sea that is like a glass pavement before God’s throne (4:6).

verse.text: And they sing the song of Moses, the slave of God, and the song of the Lamb, saying: “Great and marvelous are your works, Lord God, the Almighty! Righteous and true are your ways, King of the ages!
verse.note: The Greek word is the ordinary one for a slave, a person owned by a master, and that is what a first-century reader heard. Most English versions have “servant,” echoing the Old Testament title of honor “Moses the servant of the LORD.” The point of the title is that Moses belonged wholly to God and acted on his authority.

The scene recalls Exodus 15, where Moses and Israel sing beside the sea after their rescue from Pharaoh. Deuteronomy 32 is also called a song of Moses. The words that follow are not a quotation of either song but a weaving together of Old Testament phrases, especially from the Psalms, Deuteronomy 32:4, and Jeremiah 10:7.

The manuscripts are divided between “King of the ages” and “King of the nations,” and both readings have early support. The Greek text translated here reads “ages”; other critical editions and many modern versions prefer “nations,” which fits the allusion to Jeremiah 10:7. The King James Version’s “King of saints” rests on very slight evidence.

Greek has a single word-family where English has two: righteous and just, righteousness and justice. Many versions have “Just and true are your ways” here. “Righteous” is used so that the link with “your righteous acts” in verse 4, a word from the same family, can be heard; that word could also be understood as God’s just judgments.

text.q: Who will not fear you, Lord, and glorify your name? For you alone are holy. For all the nations will come and worship before you, for your righteous acts have been revealed.”

verse.text: After these things I looked, and the sanctuary of the tent of testimony in heaven was opened,
verse.note: Greek has two words that English Bibles usually both translate “temple”: one for the whole complex with its courts, and this one for the building where God dwells. This translation renders the second as “sanctuary” throughout. Most versions have “temple” here.

The word traditionally rendered “tabernacle” is the ordinary Greek word for a tent. “Tent of testimony” is the Greek Old Testament’s name for Israel’s portable wilderness sanctuary, which housed the tablets of the covenant, called “the testimony.” The phrase probably means “the sanctuary, that is, the tent of testimony”: John sees the heavenly original of that tent.

verse.text: and the seven angels who had the seven plagues came out of the sanctuary, clothed in clean, bright linen and with golden sashes wrapped around their chests.
verse.note: A few important early manuscripts read “stone” instead of “linen”; the two Greek words differ by a single letter. Most editors regard “stone” as a copying slip, though a few have defended it as the harder reading in light of Ezekiel 28:13.

verse.text: Then one of the four living creatures gave the seven angels seven golden bowls full of the fury of God, who lives forever and ever.
And the sanctuary was filled with smoke from the glory of God and from his power, and no one could enter the sanctuary until the seven plagues of the seven angels were completed.
verse.note: In the Old Testament, cloud or smoke filling the sanctuary marks the overwhelming presence of God. Moses could not enter the tent when the cloud of glory filled it (Exodus 40:34–35), and the priests could not stand to minister at the dedication of Solomon’s temple (1 Kings 8:10–11). See also Isaiah 6:4.

verse.text: Then I heard a loud voice from the sanctuary saying to the seven angels, “Go and pour out the seven bowls of the fury of God on the earth.”
verse.note: Greek has two words that English Bibles usually both render “temple”: one for the whole complex with its courts, and this one for the building where God dwells. Here it is the heavenly sanctuary that 15:8 has just described as filled with smoke. Most English versions have “temple”.

The Greek word names hot, passionate anger. A different word, the usual one for “wrath”, stands beside it in verse 19 (“the fury of his wrath”). Most versions have “wrath” here, though several use “fury” or “fierceness” in verse 19; “fury” is used throughout this chapter to keep the two words distinct.

The speaker is not identified. Because 15:8 says no one could enter the sanctuary until the seven plagues were finished, most interpreters take this to be God’s own voice, as in verse 17, where the voice comes “from the throne”. The voice does speak of God in the third person, and some take it to be an angel’s.

verse.text: So the first went and poured out his bowl on the earth, and foul and painful sores broke out on the people who had the mark of the beast and who worshiped its image.
The second poured out his bowl into the sea, and it became blood like that of a dead person, and every living creature died, all that were in the sea.
The third poured out his bowl into the rivers and the springs of water, and they became blood.
And I heard the angel of the waters saying, “You are just, you who are and who were, the Holy One, because you have passed these judgments,
verse.note: Greek has a single word-family where English has two (righteous/just, righteousness/justice). Because the subject here and in verse 7 is God’s judging, “just” is used. The King James Version has “righteous”, and most modern versions have “just”.

The King James Version reads “which art, and wast, and shalt be”. That wording comes from a reading introduced into sixteenth-century printed editions and has no known Greek manuscript support. The manuscripts read “the Holy One”, and modern editions and translations follow them.

text.q: for they poured out the blood of holy ones and prophets, and you have given them blood to drink. They deserve it.”

verse.note: The traditional “saints” now suggests canonized individuals or people of exceptional virtue. The Greek word is used of all members of the community as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint’s language for Israel. Many translations keep “saints”, and others use “God’s people”.

verse.text: And I heard the altar saying, “Yes, Lord God the Almighty, true and just are your judgments.”
The fourth poured out his bowl on the sun, and it was allowed to scorch people with fire.
People were scorched with great heat, and they blasphemed the name of God, who has authority over these plagues, and they did not turn back to give him glory.
verse.note: “Repent” now centers on feeling sorry. The Greek verb carries the prophets’ call to return to God, a change of direction in mind and conduct. Most translations keep “repent” as an established term that readers understand to include a change of life.

verse.text: The fifth poured out his bowl on the throne of the beast, and its kingdom was plunged into darkness. People gnawed their tongues because of the pain,
and they blasphemed the God of heaven because of their pains and their sores, and they did not turn back from their deeds.
The sixth poured out his bowl on the great river, the Euphrates, and its water was dried up, so that the way might be prepared for the kings from the rising of the sun.
verse.note: The Euphrates was the ideal eastern boundary of the land promised to Israel, and in the first century it was the frontier between the Roman world and the Parthian empire, the power Rome feared most. The drying up of waters to open a way echoes the exodus and the crossing of the Jordan, and the prophets speak of God drying up rivers in connection with Babylon’s fall (for example, Isaiah 44:27).

verse.text: And I saw, coming out of the mouth of the dragon and out of the mouth of the beast and out of the mouth of the false prophet, three unclean spirits like frogs;
for they are spirits of demons performing signs, which go out to the kings of the whole inhabited world to gather them for the battle of the great day of God the Almighty.

text.q: “Look, I am coming like a thief. Blessed is the one who stays awake and keeps his clothes on, so that he will not walk around naked and people see his shame.”

note.term: I am coming like a thief

verse.note: The narrative is interrupted by an unannounced first-person saying. Its content matches the words of the risen Jesus earlier in the book (3:3) and his sayings about the thief in the Gospels, so it is taken as his voice. Many versions set the verse in parentheses.

verse.text: And they gathered them to the place that is called in Hebrew Armageddon.
verse.note: The Greek verb is singular. A neuter plural subject regularly takes a singular verb, so the subject is most naturally the three spirits of verse 14, hence “they gathered”. It could also be read as “he gathered”, with God as the subject; the King James Version has “he”.

The Greek spelling is closer to “Harmagedon”; the familiar English form is kept here. The name is usually explained as Hebrew for “mountain of Megiddo”, after the site of famous Old Testament battles (Judges 5:19; 2 Kings 23:29). Megiddo lies on a plain, not a mountain, and the derivation remains disputed.

verse.text: The seventh poured out his bowl on the air, and a loud voice came out of the sanctuary, from the throne, saying, “It is done!”

And there were flashes of lightning, rumblings, and peals of thunder, and there was a great earthquake, such as had not happened since people came to be on the earth, so mighty an earthquake, so great.
The great city split into three parts, and the cities of the nations fell. And Babylon the great was remembered before God, to be given the cup of the wine of the fury of his wrath.
Every island fled, and no mountains were to be found.
And great hailstones, about a talent in weight, came down from the sky on people; and people blasphemed God because of the plague of hail, for that plague was exceedingly great.
verse.note: A talent was the largest common unit of weight. Its value varied by standard and period, from roughly sixty to ninety pounds or more (about twenty-six to forty kilograms). Many modern versions give “about a hundred pounds”.

verse.text: Then one of the seven angels who had the seven bowls came and spoke with me, saying, “Come, I will show you the judgment on the great prostitute who sits on many waters,
verse.note: The phrase echoes Jeremiah 51:13, where historical Babylon, built on the Euphrates and its canals, is addressed as the one who lives “by many waters.” The angel gives the waters a symbolic meaning in verse 15.

text.q: with whom the kings of the earth committed sexual immorality, and those who live on the earth became drunk on the wine of her sexual immorality.”

verse.note: The Greek noun and its verb are cognate with the word for “prostitute” in verse 1 and cover prostitution and illicit sex generally; older versions have “whore” or “harlot” and “fornication.” In the Hebrew prophets the image is used of cities and peoples for idolatry and for corrupting political and commercial entanglements, and most interpreters take it in that figurative sense here.

verse.text: And he carried me away in the Spirit into a wilderness. And I saw a woman sitting on a scarlet beast that was full of blasphemous names and had seven heads and ten horns.
verse.note: The Greek has no article and could also be read “in spirit,” meaning in a visionary state as opposed to bodily travel. The same phrase marks the main visions of the book (1:10; 4:2; 21:10), and most translations take it as a reference to God’s Spirit.

verse.text: The woman was clothed in purple and scarlet and adorned with gold and precious stones and pearls, and she held in her hand a golden cup full of abominations and the impurities of her sexual immorality,
and on her forehead a name was written, a mystery: “Babylon the Great, the mother of prostitutes and of the abominations of the earth.”
verse.note: The word may be part of the inscription itself (“Mystery, Babylon the Great,” as in the King James Version) or a comment that the name has a hidden, symbolic meaning. The second reading is followed here, as in most recent translations: the name is not literal Babylon, and the angel goes on to explain it in verses 7–18.

verse.text: And I saw the woman drunk on the blood of the holy ones and on the blood of the witnesses of Jesus. And when I saw her, I was greatly amazed.
verse.note: The traditional “saints” now suggests canonized individuals or people of exceptional virtue. The Greek term is used of all members of the community as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint’s language for Israel. Many translations keep “saints”; others use “God’s people.”

The Greek word means “witness,” one who testifies. Because these witnesses have been killed, many versions use “martyrs,” the English word that descends from it, but the narrowing of the term to “one who dies for the faith” is generally thought to be later than Revelation, or only just beginning in it. The genitive can mean witnesses belonging to Jesus or witnesses who testify to him.

verse.text: And the angel said to me, “Why are you amazed? I will tell you the mystery of the woman and of the beast that carries her, the one that has the seven heads and the ten horns.

text.q: The beast that you saw was, and is not, and is about to come up out of the abyss, and it goes to destruction. And those who live on the earth whose names have not been written in the book of life from the foundation of the world will be amazed when they see the beast, because it was, and is not, and will come.

note.term: was, and is not, and is about to come up out of the abyss

verse.note: The threefold description deliberately mimics the title of God in this book, “the one who is and who was and who is coming” (1:4, 8; 4:8). The beast is presented as a counterfeit of God, but its formula has “is not” in the middle and ends in destruction.

text.q: This calls for a mind that has wisdom. The seven heads are seven mountains on which the woman sits. They are also seven kings:

verse.note: The Greek word covers both mountains and hills, and some translations have “seven hills.” Rome was proverbially the city on seven hills, and most scholars think first-century readers would have recognized the allusion at once. A minority take the mountains purely as symbols of kingdoms or powers.

text.q: five have fallen, one is, the other has not yet come, and when he comes he must remain only a little while.

verse.note: The identity of the seven kings is disputed. Many scholars see a sequence of Roman emperors, though they differ on where to begin counting and whom to include, and many connect the beast that “is one of the seven” in verse 11 with the contemporary rumor that Nero would return. Others take seven as a symbolic number for the complete span of oppressive rule rather than a list to be decoded.

text.q: And the beast that was and is not is itself an eighth, and it is one of the seven, and it goes to destruction.
And the ten horns that you saw are ten kings who have not yet received royal power, but they receive authority as kings for one hour, together with the beast.

verse.note: The Greek word can mean a realm or the rule and status of a king. Here and in verses 17 and 18 it is something received, handed over, and held over other kings, so the sense is kingship rather than territory. Older versions have “kingdom” in verses 12 and 17 and “reigns” in verse 18; several modern versions use “royal power” or “dominion.”

text.q: These have one purpose, and they give their power and authority to the beast.
These will make war on the Lamb, and the Lamb will conquer them, because he is Lord of lords and King of kings, and those with him are called and chosen and faithful.”

verse.note: The Greek verb is the ordinary word for winning a battle or contest. “Overcome,” used by the King James Version and several modern versions, now tends to suggest merely getting past a difficulty; “conquer” keeps the note of victory and the link with the promises to “the one who conquers” in chapters 2–3. The meaning is not in dispute.

note.term: those with him are called and chosen and faithful

verse.note: The Greek has no verb in this clause. It can be read as a description of the Lamb’s companions, as here, or as saying that they share in the victory: “and those with him, the called and chosen and faithful, will conquer too.” Translations are divided.

verse.text: Then he said to me, “The waters that you saw, where the prostitute sits, are peoples and multitudes and nations and languages.
verse.note: The same Greek word is translated “Gentiles” elsewhere in the New Testament where it refers to the non-Jewish peoples. In Revelation’s recurring lists of peoples, nations, and languages, the scope is the whole world.

text.q: And the ten horns that you saw, and the beast—these will hate the prostitute. They will make her desolate and naked, and they will eat her flesh and burn her up with fire,
for God has put it into their hearts to carry out his purpose, and to act with one purpose and give their royal power to the beast, until the words of God are fulfilled.
And the woman that you saw is the great city that has royal power over the kings of the earth.”

verse.text: After this I saw another angel coming down from heaven, having great authority, and the earth was lit up by his glory.

And he cried out in a mighty voice, saying, “Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great! She has become a dwelling place of demons, a prison for every unclean spirit, a prison for every unclean bird, and a prison for every unclean and hated beast.
verse.note: Most scholars hold that first-century readers would have recognized “Babylon” as a cipher for Rome, the imperial power that, like ancient Babylon, had destroyed Jerusalem and its temple. A minority take it to be Jerusalem or a symbol of any oppressive world power. The laments that follow draw heavily on the prophets’ oracles against Babylon and against the trading city of Tyre (Isaiah 13, 47; Jeremiah 50–51; Ezekiel 26–27).

The Greek word ordinarily means a prison or a guard post, and it is the word for “prison” elsewhere in Revelation. Most modern versions render it “haunt” here to match “dwelling place” and the prophetic picture of ruins inhabited by wild creatures. “Prison” keeps the word’s normal sense; the ruined city becomes the place where unclean things are confined. Either reading is defensible.

note.term: a prison for every unclean and hated beast

verse.note: The manuscripts differ over this list. Some have only the spirit and the bird (the form behind the KJV), others only the spirit and the beast, and others all three as here. The shorter forms probably arose when a copyist’s eye skipped between the repeated phrases, but the matter is not certain.

text.q: For all the nations have fallen through the wine of the passion of her sexual immorality, and the kings of the earth have committed sexual immorality with her, and the merchants of the earth have grown rich from the power of her luxury.”

verse.note: The Greek text translated here reads “have fallen,” which is the reading of the earliest major manuscripts. Most English versions follow a reading that differs by a single letter, “have drunk,” found in fewer and later witnesses but thought by many scholars to suit the image of wine better. Others consider “have drunk” a scribal correction that makes the sentence smoother.
The Greek word here is the same one this translation renders “Gentiles” where the non-Jewish peoples are meant. In Revelation’s “all the nations” the scope is the whole world, so “nations” is used.

The word means strong feeling, and elsewhere in Revelation it usually means God’s wrath. Here it may mean the heat of Babylon’s desire (“the wine of her passionate immorality”), or the wrath that her immorality brings down (“the wine of the wrath of her fornication,” as in the KJV). Translations are divided, and some think both ideas are deliberately fused.

The Hebrew prophets regularly described a people’s idolatry and corrupting alliances as prostitution or sexual unfaithfulness. Readers steeped in that language would have understood the kings’ “sexual immorality” with Babylon as political, economic and religious entanglement with her, not literal sexual acts.

verse.text: Then I heard another voice from heaven saying, “Come out of her, my people, so that you do not share in her sins and do not receive any of her plagues,

text.q: for her sins have piled up as high as heaven, and God has remembered her crimes.
Pay her back as she herself has paid, and give her double according to her deeds; in the cup she mixed, mix her a double portion.
As much as she glorified herself and lived in luxury, give her that much torment and mourning. For in her heart she says, ‘I sit as queen; I am no widow, and I will never see mourning.’
For this reason her plagues will come in a single day—death and mourning and famine—and she will be burned up with fire, for mighty is the Lord God who has judged her.”

verse.note: In the Greek Old Testament this word often stands for “pestilence,” and beside “famine” in a list of plagues that may be its sense here. Some versions translate it “pestilence.” The ordinary meaning is kept because the Greek does not decide the question.

verse.text: And the kings of the earth, who committed sexual immorality and lived in luxury with her, will weep and wail over her when they see the smoke of her burning,
standing far off for fear of her torment, saying, “Woe, woe, the great city, Babylon the mighty city! For in a single hour your judgment has come.”
And the merchants of the earth weep and mourn over her, because no one buys their cargo anymore—

cargo of gold and silver and precious stones and pearls, and fine linen and purple and silk and scarlet; and every kind of citron wood, and every article of ivory, and every article of the most precious wood and of bronze and iron and marble;
and cinnamon and spice and incense and perfume and frankincense, and wine and olive oil and fine flour and wheat, and cattle and sheep, and horses and carriages and slaves—and human lives.
verse.note: The word rendered “slaves” is literally “bodies,” the ordinary commercial term for slaves in the Greek of the period. The closing phrase echoes Ezekiel 27:13, where Tyre trades in human beings. The “and” may add a further item or may mean “that is,” so that the list ends by naming what the “bodies” really are. The word rendered “lives” is traditionally “souls.”

verse.text: The ripe fruit your soul desired has gone from you, and all that is sumptuous and splendid has perished from you, and never again will they be found.
The merchants of these things, who grew rich from her, will stand far off for fear of her torment, weeping and mourning,
saying, “Woe, woe, the great city, clothed in fine linen and purple and scarlet, and gilded with gold and precious stones and pearls!
For in a single hour such great wealth has been laid waste.” And every helmsman and everyone who travels by ship, and sailors and all who make their living from the sea, stood far off
and cried out as they saw the smoke of her burning, saying, “What city is like the great city?”

And they threw dust on their heads and cried out, weeping and mourning, saying, “Woe, woe, the great city, in which all who had ships on the sea grew rich from her opulence! For in a single hour she has been laid waste.”
Rejoice over her, heaven, and you holy ones and apostles and prophets, for God has given judgment for you against her.
verse.note: “Saints” now suggests canonized individuals or people of exceptional virtue. The Greek term is used of all believers as people set apart for God, echoing the Greek Old Testament’s language for Israel. Many translations keep “saints”; others use “God’s people.”

note.term: given judgment for you against her

verse.note: The Greek is compressed: literally, “God has judged your judgment out of her.” It may mean that God has decided the case of his people against Babylon, as rendered here, or that God has imposed on her the sentence she once passed on them. Both readings have strong scholarly support.

verse.text: Then one mighty angel picked up a stone like a great millstone and threw it into the sea, saying, “With such violence Babylon the great city will be thrown down, and she will never be found again.

text.q: The sound of harpists and musicians and pipers and trumpeters will never be heard in you again; no craftsman of any craft will ever be found in you again; the sound of a mill will never be heard in you again;

the light of a lamp will never shine in you again; the voice of bridegroom and bride will never be heard in you again. For your merchants were the great ones of the earth, for by your sorcery all the nations were led astray.
And in her was found the blood of prophets and holy ones, and of all who have been slaughtered on the earth.”

verse.text: After these things I heard what sounded like the loud voice of a great crowd in heaven, saying, “Hallelujah! Salvation and glory and power belong to our God,
verse.note: A Hebrew liturgical shout meaning “Praise Yah” (a short form of God’s name), familiar to Greek-speaking Jews from the Psalms, where the Septuagint leaves it untranslated. Its only New Testament occurrences are the four in this chapter.

text.q: for his judgments are true and just; for he has judged the great prostitute who corrupted the earth with her prostitution, and he has avenged on her the blood of his slaves.”

verse.note: Greek has one word-family where English has two: “righteous/just” and “righteousness/justice.” Because God’s judging is in view, this translation uses “just” here and “justice” in verse 11, while the related noun in verse 8 is rendered “righteous acts.” Older versions have “righteous” and “in righteousness”; many modern versions also use “just” and “justice” in these verses.

The Greek noun is from the same root as the word for “prostitute” just before it, and the rendering keeps that echo. In Revelation the image draws on the prophets’ language for idolatry and corrupting alliances, not literal sexual conduct. Most versions have “fornication,” “immorality” or “adulteries.”

The Greek word is the ordinary term for a slave, a person owned by a master, and is the same word rendered “slave” in verse 18. Most versions soften it to “servants” when it describes God’s people. In the Septuagint it is also an honorific for those who belong wholly to God, such as Moses and the prophets.

verse.text: And a second time they said, “Hallelujah! Her smoke rises forever and ever.”
And the twenty-four elders and the four living creatures fell down and worshiped God, who is seated on the throne, saying, “Amen. Hallelujah!”
And a voice came from the throne, saying, “Praise our God, all you his slaves, and you who fear him, the small and the great.”
And I heard what sounded like the voice of a great crowd, like the sound of many waters and like the sound of mighty thunders, saying, “Hallelujah! For the Lord, God the Almighty, has begun to reign.
verse.note: The Greek verb is a past tense that can mark the start of a reign (“has become king”) or simply state the fact (“reigns”). Because the hymn celebrates God’s rule being openly established with Babylon’s fall, the first sense is chosen. Many versions have “reigns.”

text.q: Let us rejoice and be glad, and we will give him the glory, for the wedding of the Lamb has come, and his bride has made herself ready,

note.term: we will give him the glory
note.traditional: let us give him the glory

verse.note: The Greek text followed here has a future tense, “we will give.” Many manuscripts instead have a form meaning “let us give,” matching the two verbs before it, and most English versions translate that reading. The difference in sense is slight.

verse.text: and it was granted to her to clothe herself in fine linen, bright and pure.” For the fine linen is the righteous acts of the holy ones.
verse.note: “Saints” now suggests canonized individuals or people of exceptional virtue. The Greek term is used of all members of the community as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint’s language for Israel. Many translations keep “saints”; others use “God’s people.”

verse.text: And he said to me, “Write: ‘Blessed are those who are invited to the wedding supper of the Lamb.’” And he said to me, “These are the true words of God.”

And I fell at his feet to worship him. But he said to me, “Don’t do that! I am a fellow slave with you and with your brothers and sisters who hold the testimony of Jesus. Worship God! For the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy.”
verse.note: The Greek can mean the testimony Jesus himself bore or the testimony others bear about Jesus; scholars are divided, and the rendering leaves both open. In the final sentence “spirit” could also be capitalized, making the point that witness to Jesus is what the Spirit inspires in prophecy. Some take that sentence as John’s comment and not the angel’s.

verse.text: And I saw heaven opened, and look, a white horse! The one seated on it is called Faithful and True, and with justice he judges and makes war.
His eyes are a flame of fire, and on his head are many diadems. He has a name written that no one knows except himself,
and he is clothed in a robe dipped in blood, and his name is called the Logos of God.
verse.note: Nearly all translations have “the Word of God.” This translation keeps the Greek title “Logos” for the personal Word (as in John 1:1), because “the Word of God” now commonly means the Bible. Most scholars see the main background as the Hebrew Bible’s powerful “word of the Lord,” which “Word” reflects and “Logos” does not; here it fits the sword that comes from the rider’s mouth. In verse 9 the same Greek noun in its ordinary sense is rendered “words.”

Some manuscripts read “sprinkled with blood,” probably under the influence of Isaiah 63:3, where the one treading the winepress has his garments spattered. Interpreters disagree whether the blood is that of his enemies, as in Isaiah, or his own.

verse.text: And the armies in heaven were following him on white horses, dressed in fine linen, white and pure.

From his mouth comes a sharp sword, so that with it he may strike the nations, and he himself will shepherd them with an iron rod; and he himself treads the winepress of the wine of the fury of the wrath of God the Almighty.
verse.note: The Greek verb means to tend a flock and is often used figuratively of a king governing his people. The line echoes Psalm 2:9 in its Greek form, where the same verb appears. Most versions translate “rule”; “shepherd” keeps the image a Greek reader would have heard, though with an iron rod and in this context the sense is of harsh dominion, not gentle care.

verse.text: And on his robe and on his thigh he has a name written: King of kings and Lord of lords.

note.term: on his robe and on his thigh
note.traditional: on his robe and on his thigh

verse.note: The Greek may mean two places, or the “and” may be explanatory: “on his robe, that is, at his thigh,” where the garment falls across the leg of a mounted rider. The rendering keeps the wording of the Greek and leaves the question open.

verse.text: And I saw an angel standing in the sun, and he cried out with a loud voice, saying to all the birds flying high overhead, “Come, gather for the great supper of God,

text.q: so that you may eat the flesh of kings and the flesh of commanders and the flesh of the mighty and the flesh of horses and of those seated on them, and the flesh of all, both free and slave, both small and great.”

verse.text: And I saw the beast and the kings of the earth and their armies gathered to make war against the one seated on the horse and against his army.

And the beast was seized, and with it the false prophet who had performed the signs in its presence, by which he deceived those who had received the mark of the beast and those who worshiped its image. The two were thrown alive into the lake of fire that burns with sulfur.
And the rest were killed by the sword of the one seated on the horse, the sword that came out of his mouth, and all the birds gorged themselves on their flesh.
And I saw an angel coming down from heaven, holding the key to the abyss and a great chain in his hand.
verse.note: The King James Version and several modern versions have “bottomless pit”, a rendering drawn from the word’s etymology. In the Septuagint the word names the primeval deep, and by the first century it was also used for the underworld where hostile spirits are confined (compare Luke 8:31). “Abyss”, which some modern translations also use, avoids suggesting a literal shaft without a floor.

verse.text: He seized the dragon, the ancient serpent, who is the devil and Satan, and bound him for a thousand years,
verse.note: This period is mentioned six times in verses 2–7 and nowhere else in the New Testament; it is the source of the word “millennium”. Interpreters have long disagreed on whether it is a future reign following Christ’s return, a symbolic figure for the present era between his first and second comings, or a future golden age before his return. The translation does not decide between these readings.

verse.text: and threw him into the abyss and shut and sealed it over him, so that he would no longer deceive the nations until the thousand years were completed. After this he must be released for a short time.
verse.note: The Greek word is the same one rendered “Gentiles” elsewhere in the New Testament. It means peoples or nations, and in Jewish usage often the non-Jewish peoples specifically. In Revelation the scope is the peoples of the whole world, so “nations” is used, as in most translations.

verse.text: And I saw thrones, and those who sat on them were entrusted with judgment. And I saw the souls of those who had been beheaded because of the testimony of Jesus and because of the word of God, and those who had not worshiped the beast or its image and had not received the mark on their foreheads or on their hands. They came to life and reigned with Christ for a thousand years.
verse.note: The Greek says literally that “judgment was given to them”. Most interpreters take this as authority to judge, and the rendering follows that view. It can also mean that a verdict was given in their favor, echoing Daniel 7:22. The Greek does not say who sits on the thrones.

note.term: and those who had not worshiped the beast

verse.note: The Greek can be read as a further description of the beheaded martyrs or as adding a second, wider group: all who refused the beast, whether or not they were killed. The rendering leaves both readings open, as the Greek does.

The verb is the ordinary word “live”, and the form used here can mean either “they lived” (so the King James Version) or “they came to life”. Most modern translations choose the latter, as at Revelation 2:8, where the same form is used of Christ. Whether this means bodily resurrection or life with Christ after death is a long-standing dispute, tied to how the thousand years are understood.

verse.text: The rest of the dead did not come to life until the thousand years were completed. This is the first resurrection.

note.term: The rest of the dead did not come to life until the thousand years were completed.

verse.note: This sentence is absent from Codex Sinaiticus and a number of later manuscripts, probably because a copyist’s eye skipped from one “thousand years” to the next. It is generally accepted as original. The sentence is an aside: “This is the first resurrection” refers back to the coming to life in verse 4.

verse.text: Blessed and holy is the one who has a share in the first resurrection. Over these the second death has no authority, but they will be priests of God and of Christ, and they will reign with him for a thousand years.
verse.note: Most translations have “power”. The Greek word denotes the right or jurisdiction to act, not raw strength, for which Greek has a different word. The point is that the second death has no claim on these people.

verse.text: And when the thousand years are completed, Satan will be released from his prison,
and he will go out to deceive the nations at the four corners of the earth, Gog and Magog, to gather them for the war; their number is like the sand of the sea.
verse.note: In Ezekiel 38–39 Gog, of the land of Magog, leads a great coalition of nations against Israel and is destroyed by God. Here the two names together stand for the hostile nations of the whole earth. Jewish tradition also came to treat the two names as a pair.

verse.text: And they went up over the breadth of the earth and surrounded the camp of the holy ones and the beloved city. And fire came down from heaven and consumed them.
verse.note: Many translations keep “saints”; others use “God’s people”. The Greek word is used of all members of the community as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint’s language for Israel. “Saints” now suggests canonized individuals or people of exceptional virtue.

note.traditional: fire came down from God out of heaven

verse.note: Many later manuscripts read “from God out of heaven”, the reading behind the King James Version, and there are other variations in the wording. The shorter text has good early support and is preferred by modern critical editions.

verse.text: And the devil, who had been deceiving them, was thrown into the lake of fire and sulfur, where the beast and the false prophet also are, and they will be tormented day and night forever and ever.
And I saw a great white throne and the one seated on it. From his presence earth and heaven fled, and no place was found for them.

And I saw the dead, the great and the small, standing before the throne, and books were opened. And another book was opened, which is the book of life. And the dead were judged from what was written in the books, according to their works.
verse.note: A first-century reader would have pictured scrolls. The scene draws on Daniel 7:10, where the court sits and books are opened. The “books” are records of deeds, while the “book of life” is pictured as a register of names, like a city’s roll of citizens (compare Exodus 32:32 and Daniel 12:1).

verse.text: And the sea gave up the dead who were in it, and Death and Hades gave up the dead who were in them, and they were judged, each one according to their works.
And Death and Hades were thrown into the lake of fire. This is the second death, the lake of fire.
And anyone who was not found written in the book of life was thrown into the lake of fire.
Then I saw a new heaven and a new earth, for the first heaven and the first earth had passed away, and the sea was no more.
verse.note: In Israel’s Scriptures and in Revelation itself the sea stands for chaos and threat: the beast rises out of it (13:1) and it holds the dead (20:13). Its absence signals the removal of what menaces creation, not a remark about geography. The Greek verb is in the present tense (“is no more”).

verse.text: And I saw the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband.
And I heard a loud voice from the throne saying, “Look, the dwelling of God is with humankind, and he will dwell with them, and they will be his peoples, and God himself will be with them,
verse.note: The Greek noun is the ordinary word for a tent and recalls the tent-sanctuary in which God accompanied Israel in the wilderness. The verb that follows (“he will dwell”) is from the same root, so “dwelling” and “dwell” are used here to keep the wordplay. Older versions have “tabernacle”; modern versions divide among “tabernacle”, “dwelling” and “home”.

Manuscripts are divided between the plural “peoples” and the singular “people”; the plural, followed here, widens the covenant formula once spoken of Israel to include many peoples. Many manuscripts also add “as their God” at the end of the verse, and most English versions include it. The edition translated here omits it.

text.q: and he will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death will be no more; mourning and crying and pain will be no more. The first things have passed away.”

verse.text: And the one seated on the throne said, “Look, I am making all things new.” And he said, “Write, for these words are faithful and true.”
verse.note: The Greek shifts to the present tense (“and he says”) without naming the speaker. The words are assigned here to the one seated on the throne, who speaks before and after. Some interpreters think an angel interjects at this point, as in 19:9 and 22:6, where similar words are spoken.

verse.text: And he said to me, “They have come to pass. I am the Alpha and the Omega, the beginning and the end. To the one who is thirsty I will give from the spring of the water of life without cost.
verse.note: The Greek verb is plural, unlike the singular “It is done” of 16:17. The subject is most naturally the “words” of verse 5 or the “all things” being made new. Most English versions render it with a singular “It is done”, which obscures the reference.

text.q: The one who conquers will inherit these things, and I will be his God and he will be my son.

verse.note: The verb is the ordinary Greek word for winning a battle or contest, and “conquer” keeps that note of victory, where “overcome” can now suggest merely getting past a difficulty. Several modern versions also use “conquer” in Revelation. The promise that follows echoes God’s words about David’s heir in 2 Samuel 7:14, here extended to every victor.

text.q: But as for the cowardly, the faithless, the detestable, murderers, the sexually immoral, sorcerers, idolaters, and all liars, their share will be in the lake that burns with fire and sulfur, which is the second death.”

verse.note: The word can mean “unbelieving” (lacking faith) or “unfaithful, untrustworthy”. Placed next to “the cowardly” in a book addressed to churches under pressure to compromise, it probably has in view those who prove disloyal, but “unbelievers” is equally possible and is the more common rendering.

verse.text: Then one of the seven angels who had the seven bowls full of the seven last plagues came and spoke with me, saying, “Come, I will show you the bride, the wife of the Lamb.”
And he carried me away in the Spirit to a great, high mountain and showed me the holy city, Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God,
verse.note: The Greek has no article and could mean “in spirit”, that is, in a visionary state, not bodily. Most translations take it, as here, as a reference to God’s Spirit as the agent of the vision, as in 1:10, 4:2 and 17:3. The scene recalls Ezekiel being set on a very high mountain to see the restored city (Ezekiel 40:2).

verse.text: having the glory of God. Its radiance was like a most precious stone, like a jasper stone clear as crystal.
It had a great, high wall with twelve gates, and at the gates twelve angels, and on the gates names were inscribed, the names of the twelve tribes of the sons of Israel:
on the east three gates, on the north three gates, on the south three gates, and on the west three gates.
And the wall of the city had twelve foundations, and on them the twelve names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb.
The one who was speaking with me had a golden measuring rod to measure the city and its gates and its wall.
The city is laid out as a square, its length the same as its width. He measured the city with the rod: twelve thousand stadia. Its length and width and height are equal.
verse.note: A stadion was about 185 meters, so the figure comes to roughly 2,200 kilometers (about 1,400 miles) in each dimension. The number is twelve times a thousand, in keeping with the twelves that run through the chapter, and is generally taken as symbolic. The cube shape recalls the inner room of Solomon’s sanctuary, which was also a perfect cube (1 Kings 6:20).

verse.text: He also measured its wall: one hundred forty-four cubits by human measure, which is also the angel’s measure.

note.term: one hundred forty-four cubits by human measure, which is also the angel’s measure

verse.note: A cubit was about 45 centimeters, giving roughly 65 meters; the number is twelve times twelve. The text does not say whether this is the wall’s height or its thickness. The closing phrase is terse in Greek (“a human’s measure, which is an angel’s”) and most likely means that the angel used the ordinary human unit.

verse.text: The wall was built of jasper, and the city was pure gold, like pure glass.
The foundations of the city wall were adorned with every kind of precious stone. The first foundation was jasper, the second sapphire, the third chalcedony, the fourth emerald,
verse.note: The modern identity of several of the twelve stones is uncertain, since ancient gem names do not map neatly onto modern mineralogy; the stone called “sapphire”, for example, was probably lapis lazuli. The names are given here in their conventional English forms. The list overlaps substantially with the twelve stones on the high priest’s breastpiece (Exodus 28:17–20).

verse.text: the fifth sardonyx, the sixth carnelian, the seventh chrysolite, the eighth beryl, the ninth topaz, the tenth chrysoprase, the eleventh jacinth, the twelfth amethyst.
And the twelve gates were twelve pearls; each one of the gates was made from a single pearl. And the main street of the city was pure gold, like transparent glass.
I saw no sanctuary in it, for its sanctuary is the Lord God, the Almighty, and the Lamb.
verse.note: Greek has two words that English Bibles usually both translate “temple”: one for the whole complex with its courts, and this one for the building where God dwells. This translation renders the latter “sanctuary” throughout. Most versions have “temple” here; the point is that the city needs no separate house for God, because God and the Lamb are themselves present.

verse.text: The city has no need of the sun or the moon to shine on it, for the glory of God has given it light, and its lamp is the Lamb.
The nations will walk by its light, and the kings of the earth bring their glory into it.
verse.note: The Greek word is the same one translated “Gentiles” elsewhere in the New Testament, where it means the non-Jewish peoples. In Revelation the scope is the peoples of the whole world, so “nations” is used. The verse draws on Isaiah 60, where nations and kings come to Jerusalem’s light bringing their wealth.

verse.text: Its gates will never be shut by day, for there will be no night there,
and they will bring the glory and the honor of the nations into it.
But nothing unclean will ever enter it, nor anyone who does what is detestable or false, but only those who are written in the Lamb’s book of life.
Then he showed me a river of the water of life, bright as crystal, flowing out from the throne of God and of the Lamb

through the middle of the city’s main street. On either side of the river stood the tree of life, producing twelve crops of fruit, yielding its fruit every month, and the leaves of the tree are for the healing of the nations.

note.term: through the middle of the city’s main street

verse.note: The Greek can be punctuated two ways. Taken with verse 1, as here and in the SBLGNT, the river flows down the middle of the street. Taken with what follows, the tree of life stands “in the middle of the street and on either side of the river.” Both readings are widely held.

The singular “tree” standing on both banks is probably collective, a line of trees, as in Ezekiel 47:12, where trees along the temple river bear fruit every month and have leaves for healing. The name recalls the tree in the garden of Genesis 2–3, from which humanity was barred. The vision shows access to it restored.

This is the same Greek word that is rendered “Gentiles” elsewhere in the New Testament, where it means the non-Jewish peoples. In Revelation the scope is the peoples of the whole world, so “nations” is used.

verse.text: There will no longer be anything accursed. The throne of God and of the Lamb will be in the city, and his slaves will serve him;
verse.note: The Greek word is the ordinary term for a slave, someone who belongs to a master, and a first-century reader heard it that way. Most English versions soften it to “servants,” though some recent ones use “slaves.” In the Septuagint the word is also a title of honor for those who belong to God, such as Moses and the prophets. The related word in verse 9 is rendered “fellow slave.”

verse.text: they will see his face, and his name will be on their foreheads.
And there will be no more night; they have no need of the light of a lamp or the light of the sun, because the Lord God will shine on them, and they will reign forever and ever.
And he said to me, “These words are faithful and true, and the Lord, the God of the spirits of the prophets, sent his angel to show his slaves what must happen soon.”

text.q: “And look, I am coming soon! Blessed is the one who keeps the words of the prophecy of this book.”

verse.note: The Greek does not mark a change of speaker from the angel of verse 6, but “I am coming soon” can only be Jesus’s own announcement (compare verses 12 and 20). It is treated here as his voice breaking in; others take the angel to be speaking in his name. Voices shift without notice throughout this closing section, and the assignment of verses 14–15 and 17 is likewise a judgment call.

verse.text: I, John, am the one who heard and saw these things. And when I had heard and seen them, I fell down to worship at the feet of the angel who was showing them to me.
But he said to me, “Don’t do that! I am a fellow slave with you and your brothers the prophets and those who keep the words of this book. Worship God!”
And he said to me, “Do not seal up the words of the prophecy of this book, for the time is near.

text.q: Let the one who does wrong still do wrong, and the filthy still be filthy; let the righteous still do righteousness, and the holy still be holy.”
“Look, I am coming soon, and my reward is with me, to repay each person according to their work.
I am the Alpha and the Omega, the first and the last, the beginning and the end.
Blessed are those who wash their robes, so that they will have the right to the tree of life and may enter the city by the gates.

verse.note: Many later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, read “those who do his commandments.” The two phrases look and sound alike in Greek. The earliest witnesses support “wash their robes,” which echoes 7:14, and modern editions adopt it.

text.q: Outside are the dogs and the sorcerers and the sexually immoral and the murderers and the idolaters and everyone who loves and practices falsehood.

verse.note: Dogs were mostly scavengers, not pets, and “dog” was a common term of contempt for the unclean or shameless. In Deuteronomy 23:18 it appears to refer to a male cult prostitute, and some see that sense here. More likely it is a general label for the morally impure, heading the list that follows.

text.q: I, Jesus, sent my angel to testify to you about these things for the assemblies. I am the root and the descendant of David, the bright morning star.”

verse.note: The Greek word meant a gathering of people. It was the term for a city’s civic assembly and, in the Septuagint, for Israel assembled before God. “Church” is the near-universal rendering and is not wrong, but it now suggests a building or an institution. Here the word refers to the seven communities addressed in chapters 1–3.

verse.text: The Spirit and the bride say, “Come!” And let the one who hears say, “Come!” And let the one who is thirsty come; let the one who wishes take the water of life as a gift.
I testify to everyone who hears the words of the prophecy of this book: if anyone adds to them, God will add to that person the plagues written in this book;
verse.note: The speaker of verses 18–19 is uncertain. Verse 20 calls Jesus “the one who testifies to these things,” which suggests the warning is his, and a number of scholars read it so. Many others take it as John’s own solemn conclusion, and it is printed here in the author’s voice. The warning is modeled on Deuteronomy 4:2 and 12:32, which forbid adding to or taking from God’s commands.

verse.text: and if anyone takes away from the words of the book of this prophecy, God will take away that person’s share in the tree of life and in the holy city, which are written about in this book.
verse.note: The King James Version reads “book of life.” That reading has almost no Greek manuscript support. It arose in the Latin tradition, where the words for “book” and “tree” differ by two letters. It entered the early printed Greek text because Erasmus lacked a Greek manuscript for the final verses and translated them back from Latin.

verse.text: The one who testifies to these things says, “Yes, I am coming soon.” Amen! Come, Lord Jesus!
verse.note: This is the Greek equivalent of the Aramaic prayer Marana tha, “Our Lord, come!”, which Paul quotes untranslated in 1 Corinthians 16:22. It was evidently a fixed cry in the worship of the earliest Aramaic-speaking believers.

verse.text: The grace of the Lord Jesus be with all.
verse.note: The manuscripts end the book in several ways: “with all,” “with the holy ones,” “with all the holy ones,” and “with you all,” and many add “Amen.” The SBLGNT prints the shortest form, on the view that the others are scribal expansions. The matter is not settled.
